C.4 Does prompt selection help?

Prompt selection spends compute differently from dense rewards. One forward pass over 2424 candidate prompts per iteration decides which 88 prompts to sample, and scoring generates no tokens. Curriculum methods that train on prompts with predicted success near 1/21/2 use the same rule (Gao et al., 2026; Qu et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2025), so we test the rule rather than propose it. It gains on two of six models with the level 3–5 pool, Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen2.5-1.5B, and both gains replicate on fresh seeds (Table 3). The studies below probe the gain from four sides. Fresh seeds and further test sets ask whether it is real (S12, S20, S33, S34). Random choice among the same candidates asks whether it comes from the choice of prompts or from moving faster through the prompt stream (S11–S13, S15, S20). Simpler estimates of a prompt’s success ask whether the learned critic is needed (S7–S9, S22). Other models and pools ask how far the gain extends (S13, S14, and Section C.5).

The answers are consistent. On Qwen2.5-1.5B, the gain carries over to 1,5431{,}543 MATH test problems that no study had evaluated on, with an interval that also resamples the problems, and to GSM8K, which neither configuration trains on; the same holds on Qwen3-0.6B. On both models, the choice of prompts carries the gain: random choice among the same candidates is equivalent to outcome-only GRPO (on Qwen3-0.6B, +0.008+0.008 [−0.003,+0.019][-0.003,+0.019] over 1818 seeds from two studies, TOST p=.014p=.014), and it trails the filter in every preregistered primary contrast. A per-prompt success estimate near 1/21/2 carries most of the gain at BB even without a learned critic, and the critic adds an early lead. A filter built from the MATH difficulty level alone gains nothing, and dynamic sampling loses at matched tokens, because the groups it discards still count toward the budget.

C.4.1 Random choice among the candidates (S11, S12) and a Qwen3-4B replication (S11)

Table 7 lists the Qwen3-0.6B configurations that share a seed’s prompt stream and evaluation draws. Random choice among the filter’s candidates reproduces outcome-only GRPO’s mix of uniform and mixed groups, while training on fewer distinct prompts. The three critic-filter configurations train on fewer all-wrong groups than either. Target 0.850.85 trains on the same share of mixed-outcome groups as random choice and still leads it by 0.0160.016 [0.009,0.024][0.009,0.024] over eighteen seeds (higher in 1515). The share of mixed-outcome groups, which dynamic sampling maximizes, therefore does not by itself account for the differences in accuracy.

The first random-choice study (S11, seeds 0–5) left its primary contrast unresolved: random choice minus the filter was −0.017-0.017 [−0.037,+0.003][-0.037,+0.003] (Holm p=.168p=.168). Pooled values over seeds 0–17 are reported as estimates.

C.4.2 Qwen3-1.7B replication with random choice (S13)

Over all 2424 seeds, the three differences are +0.002+0.002 [−0.006,+0.011][-0.006,+0.011] (filter minus outcome), −0.004-0.004 [−0.011,+0.003][-0.011,+0.003] (random minus filter), and −0.002-0.002 [−0.013,+0.009][-0.013,+0.009] (random minus outcome). The manipulation check passed in every run. The control’s chosen prompts matched the candidates’ predicted success to within 0.0070.007. It trained on 2.52.5 [2.1,2.9][2.1,2.9] points more all-wrong groups than the filter, and the two configurations scored identical candidates in all 11,10211{,}102 shared iterations before BB. On this size the filter removes mainly all-correct groups. Over the fresh seeds, the all-correct share falls from 38%38\% to 27%27\% and the all-wrong share from 25%25\% to 22%22\%, while the mixed share rises from 38%38\% to 51%51\%.

Its chosen prompts were nearer 1/21/2 than its candidates in all twelve runs (0.5140.514 against 0.5440.544).

C.4.8 A filter without a critic on Qwen2.5-1.5B (S22)

S22 asked whether the Qwen2.5-1.5B gain needs a learned critic. Its one new configuration is the S15/S20 filter configuration with the history estimate in place of the critic: the same candidates, rule, warm-up, and random picks. It ran on the same 3636 seeds, paired with the S15 and S20 runs of each seed. The history filter has no per-prompt estimate until a prompt has been trained. A filter run scores about 15,20015{,}200 candidates before BB, 4.44.4 passes through the 3,4583{,}458 prompts of the stream, so its first pass ends near 0.23​B0.23B. Holm adjustment covered two primary contrasts:

  • •

    History filter minus outcome, with no directional prediction: +0.0060+0.0060 [0.0011,0.0110][0.0011,0.0110] (Holm p=.035p=.035; higher in 2222 of 3636; crossed bootstrap [−0.002,+0.014][-0.002,+0.014]).

  • •

    Critic filter minus history filter, predicted positive: +0.0024+0.0024 [−0.0020,+0.0068][-0.0020,+0.0068] (Holm p=.27p=.27; higher in 2121 of 3636; crossed [−0.006,+0.010][-0.006,+0.010]), equivalent to zero within ±0.02\pm 0.02 (TOST p<10−9p<10^{-9}).

Secondary results:

  • •

    Over the first half of the budget, the critic filter led the history filter by 0.0190.019 [0.016,0.021][0.016,0.021] on average, in all 3636 seeds. By evaluation, its lead was +0.020+0.020 at B/8B/8, peaked at +0.026+0.026 at B/4B/4, and fell to +0.002+0.002 at BB. Over the same half, the history filter led outcome-only GRPO by +0.002+0.002 [−0.001,+0.004][-0.001,+0.004].

  • •

    The history filter led random choice from its candidates by +0.007+0.007 [0.002,0.012][0.002,0.012] (p=.010p=.010).

  • •

    Strict-verifier accuracy: +0.017+0.017 [−0.001,+0.035][-0.001,+0.035] over outcome-only, carried by the two drifted outcome-only runs (+0.236+0.236 and +0.204+0.204 on seeds 30 and 32).

  • •

    The history filter raised mixed groups by 4.84.8 points [4.4,5.2][4.4,5.2], higher in every seed, about half the critic filter’s 9.89.8 on the same seeds.

Descriptive: its candidates’ estimated success averaged 0.330.33, and its chosen prompts’ 0.370.37. Its mean training reward before BB was 0.400.40, against 0.370.37 for outcome-only GRPO and 0.460.46 for the critic filter. It trained on 3,4443{,}444 distinct prompts per run on average, against the critic filter’s 2,6052{,}605. A per-prompt success estimate near 1/21/2 thus carries the gain at BB without a learned critic. The interval on the critic filter’s advantage at BB, [−0.002,+0.007][-0.002,+0.007], does not exclude a difference nearly as large as the critic filter’s own gain (+0.008+0.008). On this model, the critic’s clearest contribution is the early lead.

C.5 Where does prompt selection help?

The filter changes the trained groups in every setting: it raises the share of mixed-outcome groups, the only groups with a nonzero GRPO advantage, by 88 to 1919 points. Accuracy, however, rises in only some settings, so the composition of the groups does not predict the gain. On Qwen3-0.6B, the filter aimed at predicted success 0.850.85 trains on about the same share of mixed groups as outcome-only GRPO (+0.5+0.5 points, compared with +0.3+0.3 for random choice) and still gains as much as the filter aimed at 1/21/2 (Table 4). The share of all-wrong groups does not predict the gain either: on Qwen3-0.6B the target 0.850.85 cuts it from 36%36\% to 15%15\% and gains, while on Qwen3-1.7B it cuts it from 25%25\% to 10%10\% and gains nothing (+0.001+0.001, n=6n=6).

What separates the settings is how hard the candidates are. In the five settings from which we formed this account, post hoc, the critic’s mean predicted success over the 2424 candidates was 0.420.42 and 0.400.40 where the filter helped and 0.540.54 to 0.700.70 where it did not, with no overlap between seeds (Table 8). When the candidates’ mean prediction is below 1/21/2, keeping those nearest 1/21/2 moves training toward easier prompts and away from all-wrong groups; when it is above 1/21/2, the filter moves training toward harder prompts. The training reward shows the move. Wherever the filter helped, its mean training reward exceeded outcome-only GRPO’s (0.430.43–0.470.47 against 0.300.30–0.390.39), and in the six settings without a gain whose candidates averaged above 0.530.53, it fell below. Outcome-only GRPO’s own training reward, which needs no critic, separates the first eleven settings in the same way, whereas the base model’s accuracy on its first training prompts, known before training, does not.

Six preregistered studies then tested the account (Table 1). Two moved the candidates across 1/21/2 by changing the pool (S19, S21), two changed the model family (S24, S27), and two kept model and pool fixed and reversed only the direction of the move, by aiming the filter at 0.250.25 (S30, S31). Five of the six predictions held. The gain predicted on Llama-3.2-1B did not appear at BB, although the filter led at every evaluation after the first. Across all twelve settings, the filter gained significantly in four of the five settings whose candidates averaged below 1/21/2 and in none of the seven above. Candidates below 1/21/2 thus mark where a gain is possible, and on a fixed model and pool the direction of the move decides whether it appears.

C.5.1 Candidate difficulty and a test on Qwen3-1.7B with level 5 (S19)

Averaged over the iterations before BB in which the critic was in use, the critic’s mean predicted success over the 2424 candidates separated, in the five settings from which the account was formed, the settings in which the filter helped from those in which it did not (S27 later found a setting below 1/21/2 without a significant gain). It is 0.4190.419 (Qwen3-0.6B, 5454 seeds, range 0.4040.404–0.4300.430) and 0.3970.397 (Qwen2.5-1.5B, 6060 seeds, 0.3830.383–0.4090.409) where the filter helped, against 0.5870.587 (Qwen3-1.7B, 0.5780.578–0.5960.596), 0.5440.544 (Qwen3-4B on level 5, 0.5330.533–0.5580.558), and 0.7010.701 (Qwen3-4B on levels 3–5, 0.6880.688–0.7170.717) where it did not. Below 1/21/2, the filter moves training toward easier prompts and away from all-wrong groups (36%→24%36\%\to 24\% on Qwen3-0.6B, 39%→27%39\%\to 27\% on Qwen2.5-1.5B). Above 1/21/2, it moves training toward harder prompts and mainly removes all-correct groups. The level-5 study on 4B did not test this account, because 4B’s candidates there were still above 1/21/2 on average. S19, preregistered after this observation, trains Qwen3-1.7B, the model without a gain on levels 3–5, on the level-5 pool and test set (2424 seeds). Its precondition is a candidate mean below 1/21/2, and its primary prediction is a gain.

The precondition held: the candidates’ mean predicted success was 0.3890.389 (seed range 0.3770.377–0.4070.407), and the chosen prompts’ 0.4570.457. The single primary contrast, filter minus outcome-only at BB, was +0.0112+0.0112 [0.0020,0.0205][0.0020,0.0205] (p=.019p=.019; higher in 1717 of 2424; crossed bootstrap [−0.0003,+0.024][-0.0003,+0.024]). Its 90%90\% interval, [0.004,0.019][0.004,0.019], also lies inside ±0.02\pm 0.02 (TOST p=.031p=.031), so the gain is significant but smaller than two points. Strict-verifier accuracy moved the same way (+0.010+0.010 [0.001,0.019][0.001,0.019], p=.025p=.025, secondary). As on Qwen3-0.6B, the filter removed mainly all-wrong groups (45%→30%45\%\to 30\%; all-correct 17%→19%17\%\to 19\%) and raised mixed groups by 12.712.7 points [12.1,13.3][12.1,13.3], higher in every seed. The lead rose to +0.018+0.018 at 5​B/165B/16 and stayed between +0.007+0.007 and +0.014+0.014 from B/2B/2 to BB. Training started from accuracy 0.2940.294 and reached 0.4090.409 (outcome-only) and 0.4200.420 (filter) at BB. The account thus predicted a gain in a model that had none on levels 3–5, a confirmatory test of an account formed post hoc on five settings.

C.5.2 A test in the other direction: Qwen3-0.6B with levels 1–2 (S21)

S21, preregistered after S19 and S20, tests the account where it predicts no gain, at the model where the filter helped most. Both Qwen3-0.6B configurations trained on the 1,3671{,}367 MATH train problems of levels 1–2 with numeric answers (after removing 2626 that overlap an evaluation set) and were evaluated on 200200 level 1–2 test problems, with the same budget as on levels 3–5 (B=17.25B=17.25M) and seeds 0–23. The precondition was a candidate mean above 1/21/2. The single primary contrast compares the filter’s gain on levels 1–2 with its gain on levels 3–5 (seeds 0–17 of S8 and S12, Welch tt, unpaired because the two sides use different runs, pools, and test sets); the account predicts it to be negative.

The precondition held: the candidates’ mean predicted success was 0.7910.791 (seed range 0.7710.771–0.8030.803), and the chosen prompts’ 0.6560.656. Outcome-only GRPO rose from 0.7060.706 to 0.8090.809 at BB, below the preregistered headroom bound of 0.90.9. The primary contrast was −0.030-0.030 [−0.039,−0.020][-0.039,-0.020] (Welch p=5×10−7p=5\times 10^{-7}, 3232 df): the level 1–2 gain, −0.005-0.005, against +0.024+0.024 on levels 3–5. Secondary results:

  • •

    Filter minus outcome-only on levels 1–2: −0.005-0.005 [−0.011,+0.000][-0.011,+0.000] (p=.071p=.071; lower in 1414 of 2424; crossed bootstrap [−0.014,+0.004][-0.014,+0.004]), equivalent to zero within ±0.02\pm 0.02 (TOST p<10−5p<10^{-5}). Strict-verifier accuracy: −0.008-0.008 [−0.021,+0.006][-0.021,+0.006].

  • •

    The filter raised mixed groups by 19.119.1 points [18.4,19.8][18.4,19.8], higher in every seed, by removing mainly all-correct groups (57%→33%57\%\to 33\%; all-wrong 4%→9%4\%\to 9\%). Its mean training reward was 0.670.67 against outcome-only’s 0.810.81.

Exploratory: the filter trailed from the first evaluation; over the first half of the budget its mean difference was −0.010-0.010 [−0.014,−0.006][-0.014,-0.006] (higher in 33 of 2424 seeds), and at BB it had not reached outcome-only GRPO’s accuracy (Table 11). Pass@8 differed by +0.005+0.005 [−0.003,+0.012][-0.003,+0.012]. The critic’s predictions on the trained prompts were 1.21.2 points below their realized success (Table 9), which does not change the side of 1/21/2 on which the candidates fall. The account’s prediction thus held in its second direction: the model that gains on levels 3–5 does not gain where its candidates average above 1/21/2. With S19, this gives two confirmatory tests, one in each direction, of an account formed post hoc.

C.5.3 Outside the Qwen family: Llama-3.2-3B (S24)

S24 trains Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct on the level 3–5 pool and evaluates it on the level 3–5 test set (seeds 0–23). A calibration stage, which ran before the preregistration and computed no contrast, applied the S1 rules: 33%33\% of the base model’s samples were truncated at 380380 tokens, so the limit is 768768 tokens, and the budget rule gives B=8.25B=8.25M. Because the default verifier’s fallback had let outcome-only GRPO drift on three of the four Qwen models, both configurations train with the strict verifier, as S17 and S18 support; held-out evaluation is unchanged. The preregistered prediction depends on the candidates’ mean predicted success. Below 1/21/2, the account predicts a gain, tested by the single primary contrast, filter minus outcome-only at BB. Above 1/21/2, it predicts none, and a gain would contradict it.

The candidates averaged 0.6780.678 (seed range 0.6380.638–0.7180.718), and the chosen prompts 0.5850.585, so the account predicts no gain. The model did much better on the training pool than on the test set. Outcome-only GRPO’s training reward was 0.3780.378 in iterations 0–2 and averaged 0.6980.698 (0.6630.663–0.7220.722) over the iterations before BB, while its held-out accuracy rose from 0.2880.288 (strict 0.2380.238) to 0.4340.434. On the four Qwen models with the same pool, the training reward of iterations 0–2 was 0.010.01 to 0.110.11 below the initial held-out accuracy. The primary contrast was −0.0037-0.0037 [−0.0098,+0.0025][-0.0098,+0.0025] (p=.23p=.23; higher in 1010 of 2424 seeds; crossed bootstrap [−0.013,+0.006][-0.013,+0.006]), equivalent to zero within ±0.02\pm 0.02 (TOST p=7×10−6p=7\times 10^{-6}). Secondary results:

  • •

    Strict-verifier accuracy: −0.003-0.003 [−0.009,+0.003][-0.009,+0.003]. Mean over the first half of the budget: +0.004+0.004 [−0.001,+0.008][-0.001,+0.008] (p=.088p=.088).

  • •

    The filter raised mixed groups by 9.19.1 points [8.3,9.8][8.3,9.8], higher in every seed, mainly by removing all-correct groups (35%→22%35\%\to 22\%; all-wrong 8%→12%8\%\to 12\%). Its mean training reward was 0.5910.591.

Exploratory: the difference peaked at +0.007+0.007 at B/8B/8 and was negative from 9​B/169B/16 on. Pass@8 was 0.0110.011 [0.0003,0.023][0.0003,0.023] lower (Table 10). The critic’s predictions on the trained prompts were 0.90.9 points below their realized success (Table 9). The account predicted no gain on this side of 1/21/2, and none was found; S27 tests whether the filter can help outside the Qwen family.

C.5.4 The gain prediction outside the Qwen family: Llama-3.2-1B (S27)

S27 trains Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, the smaller model of the same family, with both configurations on the strict verifier as in S24 (seeds 0–23). Two stages ran before the preregistration and computed no contrast. A calibration stage applied the S1 rules: 37.5%37.5\% of the base model’s samples were truncated at 380380 tokens, so the limit is 768768 tokens, and the budget rule gives B=10.0B=10.0M. At 768768 tokens the base model’s accuracy on the level 3–5 test set was 0.1470.147 (strict 0.0750.075). A pilot then chose the training pool by a rule fixed with the calibration. Outcome-only GRPO was trained to BB with a seed outside the study, on the level 3–5 pool and on the level-5 pool. The study would use the level 3–5 pool if that pilot’s mean training reward over the iterations before BB was below 0.450.45, and otherwise the level-5 pool under the same condition. The level 3–5 pilot’s training reward was 0.3870.387, so the study uses that pool and its test set. The precondition is a candidate mean below 1/21/2; the single primary contrast, filter minus outcome-only at BB, is then predicted to be positive, and a contrast equivalent to zero or negative counts against the account.

The candidates averaged 0.4200.420 (seed range 0.3950.395–0.4430.443), and the chosen prompts 0.4670.467, so the precondition held. Outcome-only GRPO’s training reward, 0.3940.394 (0.3640.364–0.4230.423), was also below 1/21/2. The primary contrast was +0.0044+0.0044 [−0.0008,+0.0096][-0.0008,+0.0096] (p=.095p=.095; higher in 1616 of 2424 seeds; crossed bootstrap [−0.0045,+0.0136][-0.0045,+0.0136]), equivalent to zero within ±0.02\pm 0.02 (TOST p=1×10−6p=1\times 10^{-6}). At the per-pair spread observed (0.0120.012), the study had power 0.860.86 for a gain of +0.008+0.008, the size found on Qwen2.5-1.5B. Secondary results:

  • •

    Strict-verifier accuracy: +0.003+0.003 [−0.003,+0.009][-0.003,+0.009]. Mean over the first half of the budget: +0.005+0.005 [0.003,0.008][0.003,0.008] (p<.001p<.001; higher in 1818 of 2424), as predicted.

  • •

    The filter raised mixed groups by 8.88.8 points [8.2,9.5][8.2,9.5], higher in every seed, mainly by removing all-wrong groups (28%→18%28\%\to 18\%; all-correct 10%→11%10\%\to 11\%). Its mean training reward was 0.4640.464.

Exploratory: the difference lay between +0.001+0.001 and +0.009+0.009 at every evaluation after the first. Averaged over the second half of the budget it was +0.007+0.007 [0.002,0.011][0.002,0.011] (p=.004p=.004), and over all sixteen evaluations +0.006+0.006 [0.003,0.009][0.003,0.009]. Outcome-only GRPO rose from 0.1480.148 to 0.2610.261 at BB, by only 0.0090.009 in the second half, so the filter reached its accuracy at BB after 0.590.59 of the budget (Table 11). Pass@8 differed by +0.003+0.003 [−0.011,+0.016][-0.011,+0.016] (Table 10). The critic’s predictions on the trained prompts were 0.080.08 points below their realized success (Table 9). The account’s prediction of a gain at BB thus failed outside the Qwen family. The filter’s mean lead was small but positive at every evaluation, significant only when averaged over half the budget, and the interval at BB includes the Qwen2.5-1.5B gain.

C.5.5 The filter aimed at harder prompts on a fixed pool (S30)

The tests of the account above changed the pool (S19, S21) or the model (S24, S27). S30 keeps the model and pool where the filter gains most, Qwen3-0.6B on levels 3–5, and changes only the filter’s target, from 1/21/2 to 0.250.25, so that the filter trains on prompts harder than its candidates while still avoiding those predicted near 00 (seeds 0–23, 10−610^{-6}, default reward, as the comparators). The comparators are the filter at 1/21/2 and outcome-only GRPO on the same seeds (S8, S12, and S16 read at BB). Two primary contrasts, Holm-adjusted, were preregistered: T1, the filter at 0.250.25 minus the filter at 1/21/2, predicted negative, and T2, the filter at 0.250.25 minus outcome-only GRPO, predicted to show no gain. A manipulation check required the chosen prompts’ predicted success to lie at least 0.050.05 below the candidates’ on average and the filter’s training reward to lie below outcome-only GRPO’s.

The manipulation check passed. The chosen prompts’ predicted success was 0.2870.287 against the candidates’ 0.3590.359, between 0.0640.064 and 0.0800.080 lower in every seed (at target 1/21/2: 0.4680.468 against 0.4190.419). The training reward was 0.2870.287 (0.2790.279–0.2920.292), against 0.3860.386 for outcome-only GRPO and 0.4680.468 for the filter at 1/21/2, lower in every seed. All-wrong groups rose from 35.9%35.9\% to 41.5%41.5\% and all-correct groups fell from 14.1%14.1\% to 6.8%6.8\%, so mixed groups rose by only 1.71.7 points [1.3,2.2][1.3,2.2]. Both primary predictions held. T1 was −0.0280-0.0280 [−0.0359,−0.0201][-0.0359,-0.0201] (Holm p=4×10−7p=4\times 10^{-7}; lower in 2222 of 2424 seeds; crossed bootstrap [−0.041,−0.015][-0.041,-0.015]). T2 was −0.0060-0.0060 [−0.0154,+0.0033][-0.0154,+0.0033] (Holm p=.20p=.20; crossed bootstrap [−0.019,+0.007][-0.019,+0.007]), equivalent to zero within ±0.02\pm 0.02 (TOST p=.003p=.003). Secondary results: strict-verifier accuracy −0.003-0.003 [−0.019,+0.012][-0.019,+0.012] against outcome-only GRPO; over the first half of the budget, −0.002-0.002 [−0.004,+0.001][-0.004,+0.001] against outcome-only GRPO, so there was no head start. In strict-verifier accuracy the filter at 0.250.25 trailed the filter at 1/21/2 by 0.0280.028 [0.013,0.043][0.013,0.043] (exploratory). The filter at 0.250.25 drifted in 99 of 408408 evaluations, in two runs, against 11 of 414414 (outcome-only GRPO) and 00 of 414414 (filter at 1/21/2) up to BB on the same seeds; one run (seed 4) was drifted at BB. Without it, T1 is −0.028-0.028 [−0.036,−0.020][-0.036,-0.020] and T2 −0.005-0.005 [−0.015,+0.005][-0.015,+0.005] (exploratory). Training took 0.540.54 hours per run on H200 GPUs. On a fixed model and pool, the gain thus depended on the direction of the move, as the account says.

C.5.6 The filter aimed at harder prompts on Qwen2.5-1.5B (S31)

S31 repeats S30 on the other model with a replicated gain, Qwen2.5-1.5B on levels 3–5 (candidates 0.400.40, gain +0.008+0.008). The configuration is the S20 filter with the target changed from 1/21/2 to 0.250.25 and nothing else; the comparators are the S20 filter and outcome-only runs of the same seeds (12–35). The primary contrasts, Holm-adjusted, were those of S30: T1, the filter at 0.250.25 minus the filter at 1/21/2, predicted negative, and T2, the filter at 0.250.25 minus outcome-only GRPO, predicted to show no gain. Because the gain under test is 0.0080.008, the equivalence margin was ±0.01\pm 0.01, as in S28. The manipulation check was that of S30, and a secondary contrast predicted no head start over outcome-only GRPO.

The manipulation check passed, by a smaller margin than in S30. The chosen prompts’ predicted success was 0.2780.278 against the candidates’ 0.3310.331, 0.0530.053 lower on average and between 0.0390.039 and 0.0650.065 lower per seed (at target 1/21/2: 0.4580.458 against 0.3950.395). The training reward was 0.2820.282 (0.2740.274–0.2890.289), against 0.3670.367 for outcome-only GRPO and 0.4570.457 for the filter at 1/21/2, lower in every seed. All-wrong groups rose from 39.1%39.1\% to 43.2%43.2\%, but all-correct groups fell from 15.8%15.8\% to 8.0%8.0\%, so mixed groups rose by 3.93.9 points [3.4,4.4][3.4,4.4], in every seed. Both primary predictions held. T1 was −0.0097-0.0097 [−0.0159,−0.0035][-0.0159,-0.0035] (Holm p=.008p=.008; lower in 1818 of 2424 seeds; crossed bootstrap [−0.020,+0.0003][-0.020,+0.0003]), against a gain of the filter at 1/21/2 of +0.0083+0.0083 on these seeds. T2 was −0.0014-0.0014 [−0.0095,+0.0067][-0.0095,+0.0067] (Holm p=.73p=.73; crossed bootstrap [−0.012,+0.009][-0.012,+0.009]), equivalent to zero within ±0.01\pm 0.01 (TOST p=.019p=.019) and within ±0.02\pm 0.02 (p<10−4p<10^{-4}). The secondary prediction of no head start failed: over the first half of the budget the filter at 0.250.25 led outcome-only GRPO by 0.00470.0047 [0.0007,0.0087][0.0007,0.0087] (p=.023p=.023), a quarter of the filter’s lead at 1/21/2 (0.0190.019), and trailed the filter at 1/21/2 by 0.0140.014 [0.011,0.017][0.011,0.017], in every seed. In strict-verifier accuracy, T2 was +0.010+0.010 [−0.027,+0.047][-0.027,+0.047] and T1 −0.018-0.018 [−0.040,+0.004][-0.040,+0.004], both widened by drift. The filter at 0.250.25 drifted in 55 of 408408 evaluations, against 1616 (outcome-only GRPO) and 11 (filter at 1/21/2) of 408408 on the same seeds; one of its runs (seed 21) and two outcome-only runs (seeds 30 and 32) were drifted at BB. Without the filter’s drifted run, T1 is −0.0086-0.0086 [−0.0146,−0.0025][-0.0146,-0.0025] and T2 +0.0007+0.0007 [−0.0064,+0.0079][-0.0064,+0.0079]; without all three, −0.0073-0.0073 [−0.0137,−0.0010][-0.0137,-0.0010] and +0.0024+0.0024 [−0.0050,+0.0099][-0.0050,+0.0099] (exploratory). Training took 0.490.49 hours per run on H200 GPUs. The direction of the move thus mattered on a second model; the early lead shows that training on prompts harder than the candidates, while still avoiding those predicted near 00, kept a small part of the filter’s head start on this model, but none of its gain at BB.

C.5.7 Candidates, calibration, and training reward (exploratory)

Table 8 lists every setting with a critic-filter configuration and an outcome-only configuration on the same seeds, ordered by the candidates’ mean predicted success. The first studies on the level 4–5 pool (S6, S7; 66–88 seeds) were not among the five settings on which the account of Section 4.2 was formed, and S19, S21, S24, and S27 tested it; we add all of them here. Training rewards are means over the iterations started before BB, under the verifier that trained the configuration (strict for the Llama models, default otherwise). In all five settings below 1/21/2 the filter raised the training reward; it gained significantly in four, and on Llama-3.2-1B its +0.004+0.004 [−0.001,+0.010][-0.001,+0.010] was not significant. In the six settings above 0.530.53 it lowered the training reward (by 0.010.01 on Qwen3-4B on level 5, by 0.050.05 to 0.150.15 in the others) and did not gain; Qwen3-1.7B on levels 4–5 sits at 0.520.52, with the filter’s training reward 0.010.01 above outcome-only GRPO’s and an inconclusive estimate. Outcome-only GRPO’s training reward, which needs no critic, orders the Qwen settings as the candidates’ predicted success does. In the first eleven settings it separated the seeds of the settings with and without a gain without overlap; on Llama-3.2-1B it fell in the range of the settings with a gain, so it, too, predicted the gain that S27 did not find. The rewards of the first iteration, before any update, do not separate the settings: Qwen3-4B on level 5 (0.300.30) falls inside the range of the settings with a gain (0.180.18–0.350.35), Llama-3.2-3B (0.390.39) just above it, and Llama-3.2-1B (0.130.13) below it. Over a whole budget, outcome-only GRPO’s training reward reflects how quickly the model learns the pool, which its first iteration does not.

Table 9 checks the critic’s predictions against the groups it trained on. Random choice trains on a uniform draw of the candidates, so its realized minus predicted success measures calibration on the candidate distribution: it is within 0.20.2 points on all three models. On level 1–2 problems and on Llama-3.2-3B, which have no random-choice configuration, the filter’s trained prompts succeeded 1.21.2 and 0.90.9 points more often than predicted; there the critic, if anything, underestimated how far above 1/21/2 they lay. On Llama-3.2-1B they succeeded as often as predicted (+0.08+0.08 points [−0.05,+0.21][-0.05,+0.21]), so its candidates’ side of 1/21/2 is not an artifact of calibration. A prompt’s prediction correlates with its group’s success at 0.670.67 to 0.720.72, although a group has only eight rollouts. On the filter’s chosen prompts, which lie near 1/21/2, the correlation is lower because their range is narrower. The threshold of 1/21/2 in the account is therefore a threshold on realized success, not only on the critic’s scale.

C.6 Does the gain last, and can retuning match it?

Where we followed the gain over time, it was a head start (Figure 5). On Qwen3-0.6B, it peaked at 5​B/85B/8 and had mostly faded by 2​B2B (S16, S17). On Qwen2.5-1.5B (6060 seeds), it peaked at +0.026+0.026 [0.022,0.030][0.022,0.030] at 3​B/163B/16 and fell to +0.008+0.008 at BB. On Qwen3-4B with level 5, it peaked at +0.042+0.042 [0.026,0.057][0.026,0.057] at B/8B/8 (S14). A head start is a saving in compute: where the filter gains, it reaches outcome-only GRPO’s accuracy at BB with 2222 to 23%23\% fewer generated tokens and 1313 to 17%17\% less training time (Table 11). The Qwen3-0.6B gain also holds at pass@8 (+0.009+0.009 [0.002,0.017][0.002,0.017], n=54n=54), which cuts the share of test problems that no sample solves from 27.1%27.1\% to 26.2%26.2\%, so the filter does more than sharpen sampling on problems the policy already solves (Table 10).

Because the gain is a head start, a faster baseline is its natural rival, and a doubled or decaying learning rate tests it directly. On Qwen3-0.6B, doubling outcome-only GRPO’s learning rate buys as much as the filter, with and without drift (S23, S29). On Qwen2.5-1.5B, a doubled constant rate lowers both configurations and the filter’s gain holds (S28), while a rate decaying from 2×10−62\times 10^{-6} to 00 at BB brings outcome-only GRPO within half a point of the filter and removes the filter’s own gain at BB (S32). The filter’s gain is thus about as large as what tuning the baseline’s learning rate buys, which is why a claimed gain should be measured against a tuned baseline.

C.6.1 Twice the budget (S16)

On Qwen3-0.6B, the filter’s lead grew over the budget (+0.011+0.011 at B/4B/4, +0.020+0.020 at B/2B/2, and +0.024+0.024 at BB over seeds 0–17), and outcome-only accuracy was still rising at BB. S16 trained both configurations to 2​B2B on fresh seeds 18–29. Because the learning rate is constant, the first BB tokens of each run are trained exactly as in the configurations with budget BB. The primary contrast at 2​B2B was +0.021+0.021 [−0.001,+0.042][-0.001,+0.042] (p=.059p=.059; crossed [−0.001,+0.044][-0.001,+0.044]; higher in 88 of 1212). At BB it was +0.015+0.015 [0.003,0.026][0.003,0.026] (p=.019p=.019), and the change between BB and 2​B2B was +0.006+0.006 [−0.009,+0.021][-0.009,+0.021]. From BB to 2​B2B, outcome-only accuracy rose from 0.4440.444 to 0.4870.487 and the filter’s from 0.4590.459 to 0.5070.507. Strict-verifier accuracy at 2​B2B differed by +0.032+0.032 [−0.065,+0.130][-0.065,+0.130], because drifted runs occurred in both configurations. One outcome-only run (seed 25) drifted from 13​B/1613B/16 and ended with 99%99\% of its samples truncated. Its default-verifier accuracy at 2​B2B was 0.4250.425, against 0.5190.519 for the filter on the same seed. Pooling the evaluations at BB of all thirty Qwen3-0.6B seeds (0–29), the filter leads by +0.021+0.021 [0.014,0.027][0.014,0.027], higher in 2626 of 3030; adding the 2424 seeds of S34 (above), it leads by +0.017+0.017 [0.012,0.021][0.012,0.021] over 5454 seeds.

C.6.2 Twice the budget with the strict reward (S17)

Because drift affected S16’s outcome-only configuration more often than its filter configuration, S17 repeated both S16 configurations with the strict verifier as the training reward. Seeds 18–29 pair with the S16 runs (same prompt stream and evaluation draws), and seeds 30–41 are fresh. Holm adjustment covered two primary contrasts:

  • •

    Filter minus outcome at 2​B2B, both on the strict reward (n=24n=24): +0.0053+0.0053 [−0.0051,+0.0157][-0.0051,+0.0157] (p=.302p=.302; crossed bootstrap [−0.007,+0.018][-0.007,+0.018]; higher in 1616 of 2424; TOST p=.004p=.004). Seeds 18–29 give +0.001+0.001 and seeds 30–41 +0.010+0.010.

  • •

    Outcome-only on the strict minus on the default reward at 2​B2B (n=12n=12, non-inferiority at −0.02-0.02): +0.0228+0.0228 [0.0092,0.0363][0.0092,0.0363] (Holm p<.001p<.001; crossed [0.006,0.040][0.006,0.040]; higher in 1111 of 1212).

The preregistered secondary contrasts, without correction for multiple comparisons, were as follows. At BB, the filter led by +0.019+0.019 [0.013,0.026][0.013,0.026] (p<10−5p<10^{-5}, higher in 2222 of 2424; crossed [0.008,0.031][0.008,0.031]), and the lead shrank by 0.0140.014 [0.004,0.024][0.004,0.024] from BB to 2​B2B (p=.011p=.011, lower in 1717 of 2424). Over the 3333 evaluations, the lead peaked at +0.021+0.021 [0.014,0.028][0.014,0.028] at 5​B/85B/8. The filter configuration on the strict reward was non-inferior to the same configuration on the default reward (+0.003+0.003 [−0.012,+0.019][-0.012,+0.019], p=.003p=.003). The filter’s 2​B2B lead under the strict reward minus its lead under the default reward, on seeds 18–29, was −0.020-0.020 [−0.043,+0.004][-0.043,+0.004] (p=.099p=.099). Strict-verifier accuracy of outcome-only GRPO at 2​B2B rose from 0.4200.420 to 0.4970.497 (+0.077+0.077 [0.001,0.152][0.001,0.152], p=.047p=.047), with +0.412+0.412 and +0.207+0.207 on seeds 21 and 25, both of which drifted under the default reward. The filter raised the share of mixed-outcome groups trained on before 2​B2B by 10.210.2 points [9.6,10.8][9.6,10.8], higher in all 2424 seeds. In strict-verifier accuracy, the filter led by +0.018+0.018 [0.011,0.024][0.011,0.024] at BB and +0.004+0.004 [−0.006,+0.014][-0.006,+0.014] at 2​B2B. No strict-reward run drifted (00 of 792792 evaluations per configuration), and all 49,00649{,}006 training iterations of the two configurations used the strict reward. Truncated samples at 2​B2B were 28%28\% (filter) and 23%23\% (outcome-only) over the 2424 seeds. On seeds 18–29, outcome-only GRPO’s fell from 36%36\% under the default reward to 24%24\% under the strict reward, and both configurations had 36%36\% under the default reward. Training took 1.171.17 hours per filter run and 1.071.07 per outcome-only run on H200 GPUs. The gain is therefore not shown to persist to 2​B2B; Table 3 and Figure 7 give S16 and S17 side by side.

C.6.3 Twice the learning rate on Qwen3-0.6B (S23)

S23 repeats the Qwen3-0.6B level 3–5 configurations, the critic filter and outcome-only GRPO on the default reward, at learning rate 2×10−62\times 10^{-6} on seeds 0–23. Each configuration differs from its 10−610^{-6} counterpart only in the learning rate. The 10−610^{-6} runs of the same seeds (S8, S12, and S16 read at BB) share the prompt streams and evaluation draws. Primary contrasts (Holm over two; n=24n=24):

  • •

    Filter minus outcome-only, both at 2×10−62\times 10^{-6}: +0.009+0.009 [−0.006,+0.024][-0.006,+0.024], Holm p=.46p=.46, higher in 1717 of 2424 seeds; crossed bootstrap [−0.0076,+0.0259][-0.0076,+0.0259]; TOST p=.07p=.07.

  • •

    Outcome-only at 2×10−62\times 10^{-6} minus the filter at 10−610^{-6}: +0.005+0.005 [−0.007,+0.018][-0.007,+0.018], Holm p=.46p=.46, higher in 1414; crossed [−0.0105,+0.0206][-0.0105,+0.0206]; equivalent within ±0.02\pm 0.02 (TOST p=.010p=.010).

Secondary contrasts. Doubling the learning rate raised outcome-only GRPO’s accuracy by 0.0270.027 [0.014,0.040][0.014,0.040] (p<.001p<.001) and the filter’s by 0.0140.014 [0.003,0.025][0.003,0.025] (p=.013p=.013). The filter’s gain changed by −0.013-0.013 [−0.029,+0.003][-0.029,+0.003] (p=.11p=.11). Over the first half of the budget, the filter led by 0.0140.014 [0.006,0.023][0.006,0.023] (p=.002p=.002). It raised mixed groups by 9.59.5 points [8.7,10.3][8.7,10.3], higher in every seed. In strict-verifier accuracy, the filter minus outcome-only at 2×10−62\times 10^{-6} was +0.043+0.043 [−0.036,+0.121][-0.036,+0.121].

Stability (descriptive and exploratory). Up to BB, 4949 of 408408 outcome-only evaluations and 3636 of 408408 filter evaluations at 2×10−62\times 10^{-6} drifted, in 1414 and 88 runs; 55 and 33 runs were drifted at BB. At 10−610^{-6}, the same seeds had one drifted evaluation up to BB (outcome-only) and no run drifted at BB. Truncated samples at BB were 43%43\% and 42%42\%, against 36%36\% and 35%35\% at 10−610^{-6}. Strict-verifier accuracy at BB was 0.3660.366 (outcome-only) and 0.4090.409 (filter) at 2×10−62\times 10^{-6}, against 0.4100.410 and 0.4350.435 at 10−610^{-6}. In strict-verifier accuracy, outcome-only GRPO at 2×10−62\times 10^{-6} trails the filter at 10−610^{-6} by 0.0690.069 [0.005,0.132][0.005,0.132] (p=.037p=.037).
