C.6.7 Pass@kk and test levels (exploratory)

Each evaluation stores, per test problem, the number cc of correct samples out of n=8n=8. Table 10 gives the unbiased estimate 1−(n−ck)/(nk)1-\binom{n-c}{k}/\binom{n}{k} of pass@kk, averaged over problems, as paired differences at BB. Pass@8 equals one minus the share of problems that no sample solves. On Qwen3-0.6B (5454 seeds), the filter’s gain over outcome-only holds at every level of the test set. It is +0.015+0.015 [0.008,0.022][0.008,0.022] on the 7979 level-3 problems, +0.024+0.024 [0.016,0.032][0.016,0.032] on the 6262 level-4 problems, and +0.011+0.011 [0.006,0.017][0.006,0.017] on the 5959 level-5 problems. With both configurations on the strict reward, the gain at BB again holds at pass@8, and by 2​B2B it is gone at every kk. On Qwen2.5-1.5B, the gain shrinks as kk grows, and pass@8 does not differ. On Qwen3-0.6B on levels 1–2, where the filter trains on harder prompts, its small pass@1 deficit becomes a small pass@8 surplus; neither is significant. On Llama-3.2-3B, where it also trains on harder prompts, the deficit instead grows with kk, and at pass@8 its interval just excludes zero. On Llama-3.2-1B, as on Qwen2.5-1.5B, the small pass@1 lead shrinks at larger kk.

C.6.8 Tokens to reach outcome-only accuracy (exploratory)

To express the head start in tokens, we take outcome-only GRPO’s mean accuracy over seeds at BB as the target and interpolate the filter’s mean curve over the same seeds (evaluations every B/16B/16) to its first crossing of the target. Table 11 gives that crossing as a fraction of the budget, with 95%95\% intervals from 10,00010{,}000 resamples of seeds that keep each seed’s two configurations together. A resample whose curve never reaches the target counts as not reached. In the three settings of Table 11 with a gain, the filter reaches outcome-only GRPO’s accuracy at BB with 2222 to 23%23\% fewer generated tokens. The same crossing on the training-time axis, which counts the critic’s prefill and refit, saves 1313 to 17%17\% of outcome-only GRPO’s training time. At 2​B2B under the strict reward, the saving on Qwen3-0.6B is 8%8\% and its interval includes no saving. The measure depends on the slope of outcome-only GRPO’s curve near BB, not only on the lead: on Llama-3.2-1B, whose outcome-only curve had nearly flattened, a lead that was not significant at BB gives the largest saving in the table, 41%41\% of the tokens.

C.7 Reward verification and drift

When no answer is boxed, the default verifier falls back to the last number in a completion, so it also credits unboxed answers. Some runs trained on it drift away from boxing their answers; we count an evaluation as drifted when default-verifier accuracy exceeds strict-verifier accuracy by more than 0.10.1. Table 12 counts drift by study and configuration. Drift appeared mainly in long or fast training: on Qwen3-4B with level 5, on Qwen3-0.6B over twice the budget or at twice the learning rate, and on Qwen2.5-1.5B in the replication and under both faster learning rates. It affected outcome-only GRPO more often than the filter, which may have inflated the filter’s lead at 2​B2B in S16. Elsewhere it was rare. The history filter of S22 drifted in 11 of 612612 evaluations; on the Qwen2.5-1.5B level 4–5 pool, no Monte-Carlo, outcome-only, or baseline-critic run drifted (S25, S26), while the temporal-difference critic drifted at 55 of 408408 evaluations, and 22 of its 2424 runs ended drifted. On Qwen3-1.7B, drift appeared only under a length-reward term (55 of 3,7173{,}717 evaluations over all finished runs), and under that term two of three Qwen3-4B runs stopped boxing their answers, with strict-verifier accuracy of 0.1650.165 and 0.0770.077 while default-verifier accuracy stayed high. One filter run and one outcome-only run of the S11 Qwen3-4B replication also ended drifted.

Training on the strict verifier removes drift without lowering accuracy. In the studies that retrained drifting configurations on it (S17, S18), no run drifted (00 of 204204 evaluations on Qwen3-4B and 00 of 1,5841{,}584 on Qwen3-0.6B), and neither did outcome-only GRPO at twice the learning rate (S29, 00 of 408408). On the two Llama models, which trained on the strict reward throughout, 11 of 1,6321{,}632 evaluations drifted. Default-verifier accuracy was non-inferior in both preregistered tests, and strict-verifier accuracy rose, mostly on the seeds whose default-reward runs had drifted. We therefore report strict-verifier accuracy alongside default-verifier accuracy and recommend the strict verifier as the training reward.

C.7.1 Strict verifier as the training reward on Qwen3-4B with level 5 (S18)

A first check, in S9, trained three Qwen3-4B outcome-only runs on levels 4–5 with the strict verifier as the reward: against the default-reward runs of the same seeds, accuracy changed by +0.008+0.008 [−0.020,+0.036][-0.020,+0.036] (non-inferior at −0.02-0.02), and none of their 5151 evaluations drifted. S18 repeated the S14 outcome-only configuration with the strict verifier as the training reward, on the same twelve seeds, so that each run shares its prompt stream and evaluation draws with the S14 run of its seed. Held-out evaluation still used the default verifier, with strict-verifier accuracy logged. In every one of the 8,3848{,}384 training iterations, the logged training reward equals the strict reward. The preregistered primary contrast, default-verifier accuracy at BB under the strict reward minus under the default reward, was +0.008+0.008 [−0.019,+0.036][-0.019,+0.036] (non-inferiority at −0.02-0.02, p=.022p=.022; crossed bootstrap [−0.018,+0.035][-0.018,+0.035]; higher in 66 of 1212). No strict-reward run drifted (00 of 204204 evaluations, against 1616 of 204204 under the default reward). Strict-verifier accuracy at BB was 0.6310.631 against 0.5200.520 (+0.111+0.111 [−0.032,+0.254][-0.032,+0.254], p=.115p=.115, secondary). The difference comes from the two seeds whose default-reward runs had drifted (+0.627+0.627 and +0.546+0.546); on the other ten seeds it lies between −0.022-0.022 and +0.076+0.076. Truncated samples at BB fell from 17%17\% to 13%13\%, and training time per run was 2.172.17 against 2.142.14 hours.

C.8 Summary

Matching compute reverses the ranking that the per-update gradient test gives: the densest reward ranks first per update and last per token, and a learned critic, which needs no continuations, matches outcome-only GRPO within two points. The same protocol confirms a real gain where one exists. Choosing prompts whose predicted success is nearest 1/21/2 improves accuracy on two models, replicates on fresh seeds and on test problems that no study had seen, comes from the choice of prompts, and follows a rule that predicted the outcome of five of six preregistered tests. The protocol also measures that gain precisely: it is a head start worth about a fifth of the budget, comparable to what a retuned learning rate buys. A claim that a dense reward or a prompt-selection rule helps should therefore state the budget it matches, the verifier that defines its reward, how its baseline was tuned, and the models on which it replicated.

Appendix D Training-Time Accounting

Generated tokens are not the only cost of an intervention. An inference engine generates continuations more cheaply per token than a training step processes rollouts, and a critic adds forward passes and fits that generate no tokens at all. We therefore also measure training time, stage by stage, and compare configurations at equal training time.

Every run logs, for each iteration, the wall time of prompt selection (including the prompt critic’s prefill pass), generation of rollouts, credit (including Monte-Carlo continuations and the learned critic’s features and fits), the optimizer update, and the copy of the updated weights into the generation engine. Training time is the sum of these over the iterations before an evaluation; evaluation, logging, and checkpointing are timed separately and excluded. Each run uses one GPU (an H200, for every run in this section) on nodes shared with other jobs. We compare configurations only within a study or across studies run on the same GPU type, paired by seed.

Equal-time contrasts (exploratory reanalyses of preregistered runs). For each seed, T∗T^{*} is the shorter of the two runs’ training times up to their evaluation at BB. Each run’s accuracy is interpolated linearly in training time at T∗T^{*}, so the configuration that reaches BB first is read at BB, and the other is read between two of its evaluations. These contrasts stop when the faster configuration reaches its budget. A Monte-Carlo reward’s runs end before outcome-only GRPO has trained as long as it needs to reach BB, so Appendix F gives every configuration that much time in a preregistered study. Table 13 lists every contrast, Table 14 gives the time per stage, and Figure 10 shows the training curves of the Monte-Carlo rewards and critics.

Totals include the weight sync (11 to 99 seconds per run). The Monte-Carlo rewards spend most of their time on continuations (the credit stage), which the generation engine samples in large batches, whereas outcome-only GRPO spends most of its time on its many updates. A continuation token therefore costs less time than a rollout token that is also trained on, which is why the token budget charges the Monte-Carlo rewards more heavily than the time budget does. The learned critic’s features and fits add about a quarter to outcome-only GRPO’s training time, and the prompt critic’s prefill pass adds about a tenth.

Appendix E Pilot Studies of Sample Reuse and Other Estimators (S3, S4)

Two preregistered pilot studies tested ways to make dense rewards cheaper, as well as alternative estimators. They used Qwen2.5-1.5B with the protocol of S1 (MATH L4–5 pool, 380380 tokens, B=12.25B=12.25M, learning rate 10−610^{-6}) and seeds 0–2 on H200 GPUs, and compared against the outcome-only and k=4k=4 Monte-Carlo runs of S2 on the same seeds. With three seeds, these are pilots: their intervals are wide, and only large effects are resolved.

Continuation reuse at the gradient level. Training on the continuations themselves uses every generated token for training. Each continuation becomes a training sequence, with the prompt and the rollout prefix as context, and receives leave-one-out credit among the draws at its cut, in the style of SPO-tree and TreeRL. On 6464 fixed batches, measured with the gradient efficiency of Section 3.3, this was 6.4×6.4\times [3.3,18.8][3.3,18.8] as efficient as outcome-only GRPO per update with k=4k=4 continuations per cut and 3.7×3.7\times [2.1,10.1][2.1,10.1] with k=2k=2, but 0.60×0.60\times [0.31,1.75][0.31,1.75] and 0.64×0.64\times [0.35,1.73][0.35,1.73] per generated token, against 0.22×0.22\times [0.15,0.43][0.15,0.43] for the Monte-Carlo reward without reuse on the same batches. The preregistered condition for training it, a per-token efficiency of at least 0.80.8, was not met.

Rollout reuse and the VinePPO-style advantage. Accuracy at BB: outcome-only GRPO 0.4080.408, the k=4k=4 Monte-Carlo reward 0.2600.260. Four clipped optimizer steps per batch (two epochs of two minibatches, clip 0.20.2) gave 0.3370.337 for the reward (+0.077+0.077 [0.049,0.105][0.049,0.105], Holm p=.007p=.007) and 0.3490.349 for outcome-only GRPO (−0.059-0.059 [−0.102,−0.016][-0.102,-0.016], p=.027p=.027); the preregistered interaction, the change in outcome-only GRPO’s lead, was −0.136-0.136 [−0.175,−0.097][-0.175,-0.097] (Holm p=.009p=.009). The VinePPO-style value advantage (Monte-Carlo value differences alone, with V⁡(prompt)V(\text{prompt}) the leave-one-out group mean) gave 0.2580.258, equivalent to the reward (−0.002-0.002 [−0.024,+0.019][-0.024,+0.019], TOST p=.036p=.036), and 0.3370.337 with the same reuse (+0.000+0.000 [−0.042,+0.043][-0.042,+0.043] against the reused reward). REINFORCE with a leave-one-out baseline instead of the group-normalized advantage changed neither configuration materially (outcome-only 0.4180.418, Monte-Carlo reward 0.2590.259).

Process rewards from a frozen PRM. Process-supervised GRPO (adapted from DeepSeekMath) with the frozen Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B and without the verifier reward collapsed: the policy stopped boxing its answers (0.0050.005 boxes per completion), and accuracy fell to 0.0430.043 (−0.365-0.365 [−0.389,−0.341][-0.389,-0.341]). Adding the outcome reward to the process rewards did not prevent the collapse (0.0400.040). Used instead as a baseline for the outcome reward that depends only on the state, the same PRM was equivalent to outcome-only GRPO (−0.002-0.002 [−0.023,+0.018][-0.023,+0.018], TOST p=.033p=.033).

Learning rate and group size. Outcome-only GRPO at 2×10−62\times 10^{-6} and 3×10−63\times 10^{-6} ended 0.0340.034 [0.004,0.064][0.004,0.064] and 0.1110.111 [−0.003,+0.224][-0.003,+0.224] below its run at 10−610^{-6} on this pool. Neither critic form gained over outcome-only GRPO at the same higher rate, with four optimizer steps per batch, or with groups of 22 or 44 completions (every contrast within [−0.019,+0.021][-0.019,+0.021], none significant). Table 13 gives these pilots on the training-time axis.

Appendix F Equal Training Time Past the Token Budget (S35)

The equal-time contrasts of Appendix D stop at a Monte-Carlo reward’s own training time at BB, which is shorter than outcome-only GRPO’s. This study asks whether a reward catches up when given as much training time as outcome-only GRPO. A preregistered study (fixed before any of its training runs) answers this question with 768768-token completions, where 20%20\% of the initial samples are truncated instead of 73%73\%. It trains Qwen2.5-1.5B on the level 4–5 pool, with the strict verifier as every configuration’s training reward, learning rate 10−610^{-6}, 88 prompts ×\times 88 completions per iteration, B=17.0B=17.0M generated tokens, an evaluation every B/16B/16, seeds 200200–207207, and one A100 GPU per run (time axes are compared only within the study). Every configuration trains past BB, with budgets set from the time ratios of Table 13 so that its training time passes TcT_{c}, the training time that outcome-only GRPO needs to reach BB on the same seed. Outcome-only GRPO trains to 1.25​B1.25B, the k=4k=4 Monte-Carlo reward to 4​B4B, the k=1k=1 reward to 3​B3B, continuation reuse with k=2k=2 (every continuation is also trained on, as in Appendix E) to 2​B2B, and the VinePPO-style value advantage with four clipped optimizer steps per batch to 3​B3B. The primary contrasts T1–T4 compare each configuration with outcome-only GRPO at TcT_{c}, with the configuration’s accuracy interpolated linearly in training time (paired tt over seeds, two-sided, Holm over the four). They were predicted to be negative for both Monte-Carlo rewards, with no predicted direction for the two variants with reuse. The same contrasts at equal generated tokens, and at the shorter of the two runs’ training times at BB, are secondary.

Primary. Every configuration’s training time passed TcT_{c} on every seed, by a factor of at least 1.231.23, so no budget had to be extended. TcT_{c} was 1.291.29 hours (1.271.27–1.311.31 across seeds), at which outcome-only GRPO’s accuracy was 0.4670.467, up from 0.3610.361 at the start. The k=4k=4 reward trailed by 0.0330.033 [0.024,0.043][0.024,0.043] (T1, Holm p=2×10−4p=2\times 10^{-4}, lower in all 88 seeds; crossed seed-by-problem interval [−0.048,−0.019][-0.048,-0.019]), as predicted. The k=1k=1 reward trailed by 0.0110.011 [−0.005,+0.028][-0.005,+0.028] (T2, Holm p=.15p=.15, lower in 77 seeds), a difference neither shown below zero nor within ±0.02\pm 0.02 (TOST p=.13p=.13). Its predicted deficit was therefore not confirmed, so our claim about the k=1k=1 reward in training time is limited to its own training time. Continuation reuse trailed by 0.0520.052 [0.041,0.063][0.041,0.063] (T3, Holm p<10−4p<10^{-4}, lower in all 88; crossed [−0.069,−0.036][-0.069,-0.036]), and the VinePPO-style advantage with four steps per batch by 0.0110.011 [0.004,0.017][0.004,0.017] (T4, Holm p=.013p=.013, lower in 77), a deficit within ±0.02\pm 0.02 (TOST p=.005p=.005) whose crossed interval reaches zero ([−0.025,+0.003][-0.025,+0.003]). This configuration therefore matches outcome-only GRPO per GPU-hour within ±0.02\pm 0.02, while trailing it.

Secondary. At equal generated tokens, all four configurations trailed, by 0.0660.066 (k=4k=4), 0.0420.042 (k=1k=1), 0.0460.046 (continuation reuse), and 0.0300.030 (VinePPO-style), each with p<.001p<.001 and lower in all 88 seeds. At the shorter of the two runs’ training times at BB, which for every configuration except continuation reuse is the configuration’s own, the k=4k=4 and k=1k=1 rewards trailed by 0.0240.024 [0.014,0.034][0.014,0.034] (p<.001p<.001) and 0.0110.011 [0.001,0.021][0.001,0.021] (p=.038p=.038), and the VinePPO-style variant was even with outcome-only GRPO, at +0.003+0.003 [−0.008,+0.015][-0.008,+0.015] (TOST p=.006p=.006). Compared only when the faster configuration reaches its budget, as in Table 13, the VinePPO-style variant would have tied outcome-only GRPO; it rose fastest at first and then levelled off near 0.450.45 (Figure 3a, Figure 11a).

Descriptive. Training hours to BB were 0.400.40 for the k=4k=4 reward, 0.520.52 for the VinePPO-style variant, 0.630.63 for the k=1k=1 reward, and 1.581.58 for continuation reuse, against 1.291.29 for outcome-only GRPO, so in outcome-only GRPO’s training time they could generate 3.2​B3.2B, 2.4​B2.4B, 2.0​B2.0B, and 0.82​B0.82B tokens. Before BB, outcome-only GRPO spent 60%60\% of its training time on updates and 39%39\% on generation; the k=4k=4 reward spent 66%66\% on its credit stage, which includes generating its continuations; and continuation reuse spent 78%78\% on updates, which include training on the continuations (4545 seconds per iteration, against outcome-only GRPO’s 66). On the mean curves, the k=1k=1 reward reached outcome-only GRPO’s accuracy at BB after 1.25​Tc1.25\,T_{c}; the other three did not within their runs, which ended at 1.27​Tc1.27\,T_{c} (k=4k=4), 1.29​Tc1.29\,T_{c} (VinePPO-style), and 2.5​Tc2.5\,T_{c} (continuation reuse). The share of truncated samples fell from 20%20\% at the start to 9%9\% for outcome-only GRPO at BB and to between 9%9\% and 16%16\% for the other configurations at TcT_{c}. With the strict reward, no evaluation drifted (default minus strict-verifier accuracy above 0.10.1), and strict-verifier accuracy at BB was 0.0040.004 to 0.0120.012 below default-verifier accuracy. Peak reserved GPU memory was 6868–7373 GiB per run; the study took 105105 A100 GPU-hours, including a smoke test of every configuration.

Adaptations, not reproductions. The two configurations with reuse adapt published methods to our trainer and recipe. Table 16 lists what each keeps and what it changes; the differences in branch points, samples per branch point, and update rule change both the variance of the credit and its cost. These results therefore describe the adaptations, not the published methods in their own settings.

Appendix G Equal-Iteration Study: Full Results

This section gives the complete account of the equal-iteration study that Section 3.1 summarizes.

Figure 13 traces the dense reward from the gradient probe to the training result. This experiment tests whether favorable local measurements pick out a useful dense reward in a short GRPO recipe. We fully fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2024; Yang et al., 2024) on MATH problems of levels 4–5 (Hendrycks et al., 2021) for 3232 iterations, with 88 completions for each of 88 prompts per iteration. Separate probes, with LoRA and with full-parameter gradients, measure the gradient geometry on fixed batches. Training samples at temperature 1.01.0 with top-pp 0.950.95 and uses Adam with gradient clipping, whereas the reported accuracy uses greedy decoding. Greedy accuracy is therefore a different target from the expected accuracy JJ under sampling used in the local analysis. The probes also compare against a reference gradient of progress estimated from a finite number of Monte-Carlo continuations, denoted h^MC\widehat{h}_{\mathrm{MC}}, rather than against the exact population gradient (Sections H.1 and H.3).

Terms. The Monte-Carlo reward assigns each of six segments of a completion the change in success rate across it, as estimated from kk continuations. In this study, the credit is centered within each completion (MC-within in the tables), normalized, and combined with the outcome advantage as Ag+α​wg,hA_{g}+\alpha w_{g,h}. There are two normalizations: dividing by the credit’s largest absolute value in the batch (max-normalized, the default), or dividing by its standard deviation (co-equal standardization). The probes split the continuation samples into two halves: half A defines the progress reference h^MC\widehat{h}_{\mathrm{MC}}, and half B gives a candidate credit from disjoint samples. Gates act on the credit before centering. The sign-opposition gate keeps only the entries whose sign is opposite to AgA_{g}; the rollout-disagreement gate weights each segment by p⁡(1−p)p(1-p), where pp is the fraction of continuations that succeed from the segment’s end. The implicit reward is log⁡πθ−log⁡πref\log\pi_{\theta}-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, the log ratio between the current policy and the reference policy.

What the paired comparisons measure. For each seed, we compare the change in accuracy from start to end of the dense-reward configuration with that of the outcome-only configuration, using the same validation prompts and scoring procedure. Seed-bootstrap intervals describe uncertainty across seeds on these fixed prompts. Probes and training configurations are separate measurements, so Figure 12 sets them side by side rather than run by run. Matching seeds and training iterations also leaves a difference in compute, because the Monte-Carlo reward needs extra continuations from each prefix. Section 3.2 repeats the comparison at matched generated tokens; measuring the resources used by each stage is a separate validation step (Sections H.1 and H.2).

G.1 Does agreement with the reference survive disjoint sampling?

The probe computes the summed scores of each completion, the outcome gradient, and the dense-reward gradient, and then projects the gradients onto VV (Figure 15). The outcome gradient’s residual outside VV is 2×10−132{\times}10^{-13} in full-parameter space, a numerical check of the fixed-batch identity. For the MC-within reward, the strongest check uses four full-parameter probes with disjoint rollouts. Their alignments with an independently sampled half-A reference are 0.97,0.66,0.89,0.820.97,0.66,0.89,0.82, with mean 0.840.84. The larger values we also report, 0.950.95 in pooled LoRA probes and 0.960.96 in full-parameter probes, compare a credit computed from all rollouts with a reference that partly overlaps with it. Disjoint sampling removes the direct reuse of rollouts, but the reference still depends on the estimator’s finite horizon and segmentation.

Does the credit add a useful direction? The Monte-Carlo reward, the implicit reward, and a permutation of the Monte-Carlo reward within each completion all produce updates that lie largely outside VV: the part outside VV carries 0.860.86–0.950.95 of the update’s norm (Table 20). Only the Monte-Carlo reward consistently aligns with the estimated reference. The pooled alignments of the implicit-reward and shuffled rewards are −0.01±0.08-0.01\pm 0.08 and −0.01±0.06-0.01\pm 0.06. Shuffling keeps the magnitudes of the token credits unchanged, but it can change the norm of the projected gradient and the Adam step. Interpolating between an independent half-B credit and noise also links the alignment of the projected components to the cosine between the full gradient and the reference (Figure 14). Similar descriptive patterns appear across 8 checkpoints from five model families (Table 21). These probes measure raw credits before the optimizer acts on them. The next question is whether this well-aligned reward improves training.

G.2 Does the gradient test pick out a better training reward?

The outcome-only baseline improves greedy validation accuracy by +0.056+0.056 [+0.041,+0.071][+0.041,+0.071] (Table 17). At α=0.25,0.5,1\alpha=0.25,0.5,1, a prespecified expansion to n=14n=14 paired seeds supports equivalence with the baseline within ±0.03\pm 0.03: the 90%90\% intervals lie inside this margin. The result holds with Holm correction over the three configurations, under percentile-bootstrap, paired-tt two one-sided (TOST), and studentized-bootstrap tests. Smaller benefits and harms remain unresolved. At α=5\alpha=5, the paired deficit is −0.124-0.124 [−0.161,−0.087][-0.161,-0.087] (n=8n=8, dz=−2.15d_{z}=-2.15), which survives Holm correction over the nine Monte-Carlo weight configurations of the primary harm analysis (Section H.2) under both bootstrap and paired-tt tests. The deficit at α=4\alpha=4 survives only the bootstrap test. In this short training recipe, therefore, strong agreement with the reference coexists with equivalence at low weights and harm at high weights.

G.3 How do the choices for combining credit with the outcome affect the comparison?

We next test choices made between estimating the reward and applying the optimizer. The coherent and shuffled rewards behave differently at high weight. Their paired difference-in-differences is −0.128-0.128 [−0.155,−0.098][-0.155,-0.098] at α=5\alpha=5, but those configurations use different rules for combining credit with the outcome. At α=4\alpha=4, where the rules match, it is −0.074-0.074 [−0.111,−0.040][-0.111,-0.040] over five common seeds (Section H.5). These controls match the magnitudes of the token credits, but the magnitudes of the projected gradients and the actual Adam steps can still differ. Along two paired training runs, agreement with the reference remains high both in the low-weight configuration and in the degrading high-weight configuration (minimum 0.9690.969 against the strict half-B reference; Figure 16). Agreement thus stays high while accuracy falls, which points to how the credit is combined and how the optimizer acts, rather than to a decay in alignment, as questions for further study.

Can gating help? A prespecified expansion of the sign-opposition gate at α=1\alpha=1 gives +0.008+0.008 [−0.004,+0.021][-0.004,+0.021] against its matched outcome-only control (n=32n=32, one-sided paired-tt p=0.100p=0.100, dz=0.23d_{z}=0.23; Table 18). The expansion includes eight exploratory seeds, and its interval includes a gain of 2.12.1 percentage points. The smaller gate comparisons are descriptive. The sign-opposition configuration at α=3\alpha=3 gives +0.036+0.036 [−0.013,+0.080][-0.013,+0.080], on the same validation prompts and scoring procedure as its outcome-only control; no matched ungated comparison is available. Rollout-disagreement gating improves on the ungated reward with the same rule by +0.056+0.056 [+0.007,+0.094][+0.007,+0.094] at α=3\alpha=3 (n=5n=5), but the paired-tt test does not exclude zero (p=0.089p=0.089). Masking changes the total amount of credit as well as where it is placed, and centering afterward can put credit back on the masked positions (Section G.5).

G.4 How does the result vary across recipes?

Finally, we check how far the pattern extends. The Qwen2.5-7B sweep has 4343 dense runs, with 33–55 seeds per configuration. No dense-reward configuration’s mean gain exceeds that of the outcome-only baseline, which itself gains 0.210.21, and the instability at high weights varies by seed (Table 23). SmolLM3-3B (n=10n=10 for the outcome-only configuration and the configurations at α=0.5\alpha=0.5 and 55) and a small NuminaMath study show similar point estimates at lower statistical resolution (Tables 24 and 26). The single-seed Phi-4 pilots are positive, with paired gains of +0.093+0.093 and +0.080+0.080 at α=0.5\alpha=0.5 and 55 (Section H.4). These positive pilots show why each recipe needs its own replication.

Do the reward source and the rollout budget matter? With co-equal standardization, the Monte-Carlo reward also gives a small difference at low weight and a deficit at high weight (n=5n=5; Table 22). An ablation of the implicit reward with a frozen reference shows a large loss in accuracy (dz=−7.81d_{z}=-7.81, n=3n=3, descriptive). The implicit reward uses the current policy in its numerator, whereas PRIME uses a separately trained implicit PRM (Cui et al., 2026). A frozen PRM trained on step labels also fails to improve accuracy when converted to credit centered within each completion, but its segmentation differs from the PRM’s native setup and its scoring head was rebuilt, which limits this comparison (Table 25). Finally, a 2020-iteration sweep over k∈{2,6,16}k\in\{2,6,16\} continuations at α=1\alpha=1 (n=4n=4) detects no improvement at those budgets. Noise in the estimator remains a possible contributor, although in the matched-compute recipe continuation sampling contributes only 4%4\% of the second moment of the k=4k=4 update (Section 3.2). In the primary short-horizon recipe, then, high agreement between the gradient and the reference did not by itself pick out a reward that beat the declared margin, which is why the matched-compute studies of Appendix C measure training outcomes directly.

Compute. The equal-iteration experiments of Section 3.1 used a node with eight H100-80GB GPUs. A 1212-iteration probe on one GPU takes about 2020 minutes, a 3232-iteration training run for the 1.51.5B model takes 11–22 GPU-hours, and a 77B run on two GPUs takes 44–66 GPU-hours. The 2727B/3535B Qwen3.6 and 2020B probes use two-GPU sharding for inference, and the equal-iteration study as a whole, with its ablations of weight, continuation budget, combination rule, and model family, used a few hundred GPU-hours. The matched-compute studies of Section 2.3 used one GPU per run (an H200 for all but 2222 of about 1,3201{,}320 GPU-hours) and report training time per run (Appendix C). A systems-performance evaluation would also need the runtime and memory of each stage.

G.5 Gate protocols and comparisons

Gates test whether concentrating the credit on the segments where it should matter most helps: the opposition gate keeps the credit that opposes the outcome advantage, and the disagreement gate favors segments whose continuations disagree.

The Monte-Carlo gates use the Qwen2.5-1.5B full-fine-tuning recipe: 3232 iterations, 88 prompts, group size 88, learning rate 10−510^{-5}, no KL penalty, six segments, and k=4k=4 continuations. The opposition gate keeps the entries whose sign is opposite to AgA_{g}, and the disagreement gate weights each segment by p⁡(1−p)p(1-p), where pp is the fraction of continuations that succeed. Both are applied before centering and normalization. We normalize the peak credit within each configuration, which does not match the total credit mass, the norm of the projected gradient, or the size of the actual optimizer step across configurations. Centering also changes which positions have nonzero credit. We trained no control that keeps the entries agreeing with the outcome’s sign while preserving the mask.

Expanded opposition gate. The pilot at α=1\alpha=1 gave a paired mean of +0.013+0.013 (dz=0.35d_{z}=0.35), with four of eight differences negative. We fixed the analysis plan before adding seeds and then analyzed the combined result, with n=32n=32, once. All 6464 dense and control runs reached iteration 3131. The paired mean is +0.008+0.008, with 95%95\% bootstrap interval [−0.004,+0.021][-0.004,+0.021], one-sided t31=1.31t_{31}=1.31, p=0.100p=0.100, and dz=0.23d_{z}=0.23; 13/3213/32 differences are negative. No gated run meets the collapse criterion, a drop of 0.150.15 from peak to final accuracy; the largest drop is 0.0670.067. The expansion includes the eight pilot seeds. Its post hoc power at the observed effect is 0.370.37, and the interval remains compatible with an improvement of 2.12.1 points.

Other opposition weights. On the same 150150-problem evaluation set and against matched outcome controls, α=0.5,2,3\alpha=0.5,2,3 give respectively +0.015+0.015 [−0.043,+0.073][-0.043,+0.073] (n=4n=4), +0.013+0.013 [−0.048,+0.075][-0.048,+0.075] (n=4n=4), and +0.036+0.036 [−0.013,+0.080][-0.013,+0.080] (n=3n=3, dz=0.76d_{z}=0.76). A fourth α=3\alpha=3 seed stopped at iteration 88 and is excluded. All eleven completed runs remain below the collapse-event threshold (largest drop 0.0800.080). These exploratory comparisons are not corrected for multiple comparisons.

Disagreement versus ungated reward. At α=3\alpha=3, both rewards use the same max-normalized combination rule, six segments, k=4k=4, 200200-problem evaluation, and seeds 00–44. Their paired difference is +0.056+0.056 [+0.007,+0.094][+0.007,+0.094], dz=1.00d_{z}=1.00. The reported paired differences are −0.035,+0.050,+0.070,+0.080,+0.115-0.035,+0.050,+0.070,+0.080,+0.115; a paired-tt test gives t4=2.23t_{4}=2.23, p=0.089p=0.089. The difference grows from +0.006+0.006 at iteration 1515 to +0.029+0.029 at 2323 and +0.056+0.056 at 3131. At α=1\alpha=1, the matched difference is +0.021+0.021 [+0.005,+0.033][+0.005,+0.033] (all 555^{5} bootstrap resamples), dz=1.13d_{z}=1.13, four of five differences positive, with t4=2.54t_{4}=2.54, p=0.064p=0.064. That configuration’s difference against outcome is +0.009+0.009 [−0.022,+0.047][-0.022,+0.047], dz=0.21d_{z}=0.21. Both comparisons are exploratory, use five seeds, and have no correction for multiple comparisons. They change the mask while keeping the recipe fixed, but they do not hold the size of the resulting gradient or optimizer step fixed.

Appendix H Language-model setup and implementation

H.1 Policy, data, and training recipe

Training and evaluation. The main policy is Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct. LoRA probes train rank-1616 adapters (adapter scale 3232) on query and value projections; the main training study updates all parameters. Each iteration samples eight completions for each of eight prompts, using temperature 1.01.0, top-pp 0.950.95, and at most 380380 new tokens. Adam uses β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.999\beta_{2}=0.999, no weight decay, constant learning rate, global gradient-norm clipping at 1.01.0, and bfloat16 weights. There is one on-policy gradient step per iteration, no inner-epoch loop, and no importance-ratio clipping. Dense weights stay constant throughout each run. The six-segment end-task credits use up to 200200 continuation tokens per prefix.

The verifier extracts the last number inside the final \boxed{}, then falls back to the last number after #### or the last number in the completion. It strips a <think> prefix and uses numerical tolerance 10−410^{-4}, or exact string matching otherwise. The same verifier scores continuations. Validation uses greedy decoding. The reported greedy accuracy and the expected accuracy under sampling therefore measure different quantities. Because of top-pp sampling, finite continuation length, fixed segmentation, and the initial success prior, the probe reference also differs from an exact population gradient.

Probe and full-fine-tuning configurations. Five geometry runs train LoRA for 1212 iterations at learning rate 10−510^{-5} on MATH L3–5 with a KL-to-initial-policy penalty 0.040.04 (k3k_{3} estimator) and k=6k=6 continuations, split three per half. We measure every reward gradient at the same checkpoints from outcome-only training. Three-seed LoRA accuracy runs use the same horizon, learning rate, and KL penalty, with 120120 validation prompts. Full-parameter probes and full fine-tuning omit the KL penalty. Main full fine-tuning uses 3232 iterations, learning rate 10−510^{-5}, a 568568-problem MATH L4–5 training pool, and a 200200-problem MATH L3–5 evaluation set. Gains are the recorded final-minus-start accuracy (iteration 3131 minus iteration 00). An initial recipe check gave outcome gain +0.052+0.052 [+0.031,+0.074][+0.031,+0.074]; the larger n=14n=14 baseline gives +0.056+0.056 [+0.041,+0.071][+0.041,+0.071]. At learning rate 2×10−62\times 10^{-6} and in the reported GSM8K control, the outcome baseline does not measurably improve.

Rules for combining credit with the outcome. Co-equal standardization scales the outcome and dense terms separately. The main Monte-Carlo configuration at α=5\alpha=5 uses co-equal standardization, whereas the other primary weights and the shuffled controls use the max-normalized rule. Comparisons with outcome-only GRPO remain well defined, because it has no dense term to combine, but comparisons between dense-reward configurations must account for this difference in rules.

Model identifiers. The eight-checkpoint probe panel uses Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Qwen/Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct, Qwen/Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct, HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct, microsoft/Phi-3.5-mini-instruct, openai/gpt-oss-20b, Qwen/Qwen3.6-27B, and Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. The final two rows use one seed and are descriptive. Larger models use two-GPU sharding. The panel reports measurements at these checkpoints.

H.2 Statistical reporting

Unless stated otherwise, end-task intervals are 95%95\% percentile-bootstrap intervals with 10410^{4} seed resamples. A gain row resamples per-seed final-minus-start gains; a paired row resamples same-seed dense-minus-outcome differences. These intervals describe uncertainty across seeds on the fixed validation examples. The standardized paired effect is dz=Δ¯/sΔd_{z}=\overline{\Delta}/s_{\Delta}, without a small-sample correction. Reported bootstrap pp values are twice the proportion of resampled means on the opposite side of zero. Because such pp values can overstate the evidence when nn is small, we give paired-tt sensitivity checks for the principal claims. Brackets denote intervals; ±\pm denotes the sample SD unless explicitly labeled SE. SD uses the n−1n-1 variance denominator; SE=SD/n\mathrm{SE}=\mathrm{SD}/\sqrt{n}.

Small samples. At n=3n=3, a 95%95\% percentile-bootstrap interval equals the observed minimum and maximum (an all-one-seed resample has probability 3−3=0.037>0.0253^{-3}=0.037>0.025), so these rows describe the observed range. For the n=6n=6, α=3\alpha=3 transition, exhaustive enumeration of all 66=46,6566^{6}=46{,}656 resamples gives [−0.108,+0.001][-0.108,+0.001], and the paired-tt test gives t5=−2.01t_{5}=-2.01, p=0.101p=0.101, with five of six differences negative. For the other paired rows with n≤7n\leq 7, exhaustive enumeration does not change whether the interval crosses zero. Probe rows pooled across checkpoints are correlated, so their spread is descriptive.

Groups of comparisons and registration. The primary harm analysis includes nine Monte-Carlo weight configurations on the Qwen2.5-1.5B, 200200-problem, iteration-3131 recipe: five in Table 17, two transition weights, and two co-equal-standardization configurations in Table 22. The three low-weight equivalence tests form a separate Holm family. This group of comparisons excludes other models, datasets, evaluation sets, and the 2020-iteration estimator sweep; the source study has 3131 Monte-Carlo configurations at iteration 3131 (3030 after merging two with the same configuration), 2222 of them outside the nine-configuration family. Analysis plans were locked before adding data for the low-weight seed expansion, complementary-prover confirmation, SmolLM3 expansion, and n=32n=32 gate expansion. The primary low-weight expansion adds seeds 88–1313 or 55–1313 to existing configurations; the gate expansion retains its eight pilot seeds. Because the expansions add seeds to existing configurations, they extend those configurations rather than replicate them independently.

Additional drift seeds. Two completed α=5\alpha=5 drift-probe seeds extend the paired estimate from −0.124-0.124 [−0.161,−0.087][-0.161,-0.087], dz=−2.15d_{z}=-2.15, n=8n=8, to −0.123-0.123 [−0.153,−0.093][-0.153,-0.093], dz=−2.40d_{z}=-2.40, n=10n=10. One eligible α=0.5\alpha=0.5 co-equal-standardization seed changes −0.004-0.004 [−0.032,+0.034][-0.032,+0.034] to +0.001+0.001 [−0.026,+0.033][-0.026,+0.033]; its second drift run stops at iteration 2020 and is excluded under the stated iteration-2828 admission rule. Drift seeds use their own outcome controls run at the same time. These runs serve as a sensitivity analysis; the nine-configuration family and the seed sets of the main tables are unchanged.

Validation sets. The main 200200-problem MATH L3–5 set is used for the weight sweep, low-weight equivalence, PRM, implicit-reward, and disagreement-versus-ungated comparisons. A 150150-problem L4–5 set is used for opposition gates, prover, and cross-family configurations. A separate 115115-problem set is used only for the degenerate-slice ablation. Starting accuracies differ: Qwen2.5-1.5B/OLMo-2 means are 0.240.24–0.260.26 on the 200200-problem set and 0.150.15–0.200.20 on the 150150-problem set; SmolLM3 starts at 0.320.32–0.340.34, Phi-4-mini at 0.250.25, NuminaMath at 0.280.28–0.290.29, and the degenerate slice at 0.030.03–0.100.10. We therefore compare configurations only within an evaluation set. Table 18 uses the available opposition estimate from the same evaluation set and omits the unmatched ungated comparison.

Deficits and collapse events. A negative paired configuration mean is different from a collapse within one run. We define a collapse event descriptively as final accuracy at least 0.150.15 below that run’s peak. We chose this threshold after inspecting variation in baseline drops. At 1.51.5B, the Monte-Carlo α=5\alpha=5 and 44 configurations have 0/80/8 and 0/60/6 such events; their largest drops are 0.140.14 and 0.110.11, versus 0.0550.055 for outcome-only. Still, all eight and six seeds have negative absolute gains and paired differences. One of five α=3\alpha=3 co-equal-standardization seeds has a drop exactly 0.1500.150. One α=5\alpha=5 and two α=4\alpha=4 seeds peak at iteration 00, so a rise-then-decay trajectory does not describe every deficit. Across 8585 eligible gate/control runs (8686 launched, one stopping at iteration 88), no drop reaches 0.150.15; the largest is 0.0800.080.

Per-configuration bootstrap values. For Table 17, the two-sided bootstrap pp values are 0.638,0.740,0.7140.638,0.740,0.714 at α=0.25,0.5,1\alpha=0.25,0.5,1, below 10−310^{-3} at 4,54,5, and 0.3040.304 for the shuffled control. For Table 22, they are 0.014,0.0600.014,0.060 for weights 2,32,3; 0.747,0.00040.747,0.0004 for co-equal-standardization weights 0.5,30.5,3; 0.134,0.390,0.2480.134,0.390,0.248 for shuffled weights 1,3,41,3,4; and below 10−310^{-3} for the three-seed implicit-reward row.

H.3 Gradient probes

This subsection describes how the gradient tests of Section 2.4 are computed at language-model scale.

Score-gradient map. At a fixed checkpoint, we compute a credit gradient with one weighted backward pass:

grad(w)=∇θ∑n,twn,t 1[generated]logπθ(an,t).\operatorname{grad}(w)=\nabla_{\theta}\sum_{n,t}w_{n,t}\,\mathbf{1}[\mathrm{generated}]\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{n,t}).

We accumulate gradients over completion microbatches using logsumexp token probabilities. The probe builds VV from at most 2424 completions and forms goutg_{\mathrm{out}} from the same subsample, so the least-squares projection uses this fixed, subsampled VV. It costs O⁡(N)O(N) forward passes, with the backward graphs kept in memory. The reported outcome residual 0.012±0.0080.012\pm 0.008 checks the numerical projection rather than the theorem itself; with full-parameter gradients, the residuals are as small as 2×10−132\times 10^{-13}.

Progress reference and sample overlap. Following Monte-Carlo prefix-value methods (Kazemnejad et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024), the probe uses three interior cuts and the endpoint, with up to 200200 continuation tokens, temperature 1.01.0, top-pp 0.950.95, and initial success prior 0.50.5. Each segment’s credit is the change in success rate across it. Half A of the continuations defines h^MC\widehat{h}_{\mathrm{MC}}, and half B, where labeled, provides a candidate credit from disjoint samples. The credit computed from all rollouts, which the primary pooled measurement uses, overlaps with half A. After projection, it differs from the centered full credit only by the projection residual (agreement within 1.4×10−31.4\times 10^{-3} over 135135 rows), so the reported agreement with the reference, 0.950.95, uses overlapping samples. The full-parameter alignments using disjoint samples are 0.97,0.66,0.89,0.820.97,0.66,0.89,0.82, mean 0.840.84. The overlapping full-parameter mean is 0.960.96, with mean±1.96\pm 1.96SE interval [0.92,0.99][0.92,0.99] (percentile bootstrap [0.92,0.98][0.92,0.98]), shuffled mean −0.05-0.05, and off-VV fraction 0.930.93.

Controls and interpolation. Permuting values within each completion preserves the distribution of token-credit magnitudes. It does not, in general, preserve ‖P⟂​S⊤​w‖\|P_{\!\perp}S^{\top}w\|, because the Gram matrix of the scores is not isotropic, and it need not preserve the actual Adam step. The interpolation family is wλ=λ​mc^B+(1−λ)​ξw_{\lambda}=\lambda\widehat{\mathrm{mc}}_{B}+(1-\lambda)\xi, λ∈{0,1/4,1/2,3/4,1}\lambda\in\{0,1/4,1/2,3/4,1\}, with unit-normalized, zero-sum half-B and Gaussian rewards. The fractions of their updates that lie outside VV are similar, but their budgets are not exactly matched. The reported within-bin and magnitude-adjusted correlations are 0.88​[0.84,0.92]0.88\,[0.84,0.92] and 0.90​[0.85,0.94]0.90\,[0.85,0.94]; the aligned-minus-shuffled reference-cosine gap is +0.97​[+0.93,+1.01]+0.97\,[+0.93,+1.01]. These measurements describe agreement with the measured reference at fixed probes.

Implicit reward. This credit is wn,t=log⁡πθ​(an,t)−log⁡πref​(an,t)w_{n,t}=\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{n,t})-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(a_{n,t}), with the actor itself in the numerator and the initial policy in the denominator. We do not scale it in the probes, because the cosine and the fraction outside VV do not depend on scale. Averaged over each run, the cosines of the five runs stabilized by a KL penalty are −0.05,+0.06,+0.01,+0.01,+0.10-0.05,+0.06,+0.01,+0.01,+0.10; without the KL penalty, values at single checkpoints reach ±0.77\pm 0.77, so alignment with the estimated reference can change sign. At initialization, the credit is zero because the actor and the reference are the same, so these summaries use only iterations after the first. This implicit reward differs from PRIME’s separate implicit PRM trained with outcome labels (Cui et al., 2026).

H.4 End-task results and controls

This subsection gives the end-task results behind Section 3.1, with the checks behind each claim.

Choice of recipe. A short LoRA recipe and a GSM8K recipe barely improved the outcome-only baseline, so they could not separate the rewards; the main study therefore uses full fine-tuning on MATH.

Low-weight equivalence. At n=14n=14 paired seeds, the 90%90\% percentile-bootstrap intervals for α=0.25,0.5,1\alpha=0.25,0.5,1 are respectively [−0.023,+0.014][-0.023,+0.014], [−0.020,+0.013][-0.020,+0.013], and [−0.016,+0.010][-0.016,+0.010], with TOST p=0.0095,0.0033,0.0004p=0.0095,0.0033,0.0004. All pass Holm correction over the three configurations at the ±0.03\pm 0.03 margin. Paired-tt TOST gives p=0.025,0.012,0.003p=0.025,0.012,0.003, also passing Holm, and studentized-bootstrap 90%90\% intervals also lie inside the margin. The reported minimum effects detectable by superiority tests are 0.0250.025–0.0350.035 at 80%80\% power; estimated power at an effect equal to the margin ranges from 0.670.67 to 0.920.92. These results support equivalence at the stated resolution.

High-weight deficits. The α=5\alpha=5 deficit remains significant after bootstrap and paired-tt Holm correction over all nine primary weight configurations. The α=4\alpha=4 deficit passes bootstrap Holm correction but misses the paired-tt step (p=0.0065p=0.0065 versus threshold 0.00630.0063). Unadjusted one-sided paired-tt values are 0.00330.0033 and 0.000250.00025 for α=4,5\alpha=4,5; studentized-bootstrap 95%95\% intervals are [−0.155,−0.026][-0.155,-0.026] and [−0.172,−0.074][-0.172,-0.074]. Using only seven configurations for correction would change the α=4\alpha=4 conclusion, but the reported claim uses all nine. The co-equal-standardization α=3\alpha=3 configuration passes the bootstrap correction, while the α=2\alpha=2 transition passes only the uncorrected test. The implicit-reward row has n=3n=3 and dz=−7.81d_{z}=-7.81, so it remains descriptive despite its large deficit.

Curve summaries. We reanalyze the n=14n=14 low-weight runs with three measures: iterations to first reach the baseline’s mean final accuracy 0.3080.308 (baseline median 20/3220/32 iterations), area under the accuracy curve relative to start (baseline +0.038+0.038), and per-run peak (baseline mean 0.3240.324). The paired dense-minus-outcome estimates, in that order, are:

  • •

    α=0.25\alpha=0.25: −0.1-0.1 [−4.0,+3.3][-4.0,+3.3] iterations, −0.001-0.001 [−0.014,+0.014][-0.014,+0.014] area, and −0.008-0.008 [−0.018,+0.003][-0.018,+0.003] peak.

  • •

    α=0.5\alpha=0.5: −0.2-0.2 [−6.3,+6.1][-6.3,+6.1], +0.000+0.000 [−0.013,+0.013][-0.013,+0.013], and +0.002+0.002 [−0.008,+0.013][-0.008,+0.013].

  • •

    α=1\alpha=1: +4.4+4.4 [−0.7,+9.4][-0.7,+9.4] (dz=0.44d_{z}=0.44), −0.007-0.007 [−0.019,+0.006][-0.019,+0.006], and −0.004-0.004 [−0.014,+0.005][-0.014,+0.005].

These post hoc summaries detect no speed advantage. Runs that never reach the target are coded as 3232 iterations, so the time-to-target statistic is censored.

Continuation-budget sweep. At α=1\alpha=1, the k∈{2,6,16}k\in\{2,6,16\} study has four seeds per setting and ends at iteration 1919 for all twelve runs. No 3232-iteration comparison is available. It detects no difference at that horizon. A separate co-equal-standardization α=1\alpha=1 set also ends before the primary iteration-3131 horizon; neither short study is included in the nine-configuration group of comparisons.

Positive pilots. The Phi-4 outcome-only configuration has three seeds and mean gain +0.142+0.142. Its dense α=0.5\alpha=0.5 and 55 configurations each have one seed, with same-seed paired gains +0.093+0.093 and +0.080+0.080. These positive pilots exceed the primary equivalence margin but provide no seed-level uncertainty estimate. They remain unconfirmed, but they limit any broad negative claim.

Qwen2.5-7B sweep. Full fine-tuning uses two GPUs, six completions for each of six prompts, 3232 iterations, learning rate 10−510^{-5}, and 150150 validation prompts. Seeds 00–44 are used except at α=4\alpha=4, which has seeds 00–22. The outcome baseline gains +0.209+0.209, while no dense-reward configuration mean exceeds it across 4343 dense runs and weights up to 2424. The descriptive collapse-event count is 3/53/5 at each of α=5,8\alpha=5,8, versus 0/50/5 for outcome-only (largest baseline drop 0.110.11). One seed at each weight ends at zero accuracy after peaks 0.460.46 and 0.430.43. High-weight seeds that do not collapse stay close enough to the baseline that configuration means at α=12,16,24\alpha=12,16,24 remain positive. Expanding the high-weight configurations from three to five seeds increased event counts and changed the α=5\alpha=5 mean gain from positive to negative.

H.5 Controls for interpreting performance loss

The high-weight deficits raise a question: why does a reward that aligns well with the reference hurt training? These controls check the most direct explanations: a decay of alignment during training, where the credit falls, the coherence of the credit, and changes in length and entropy.

Alignment along training. Paired full-fine-tuning runs at α=0.5,5\alpha=0.5,5, two seeds each, save checkpoints every four iterations. Full-parameter probes use G=16G=16, k=10k=10. The alignment between the full credit and the overlapping half-A reference stays at or above 0.9920.992 (from 0.9930.993 to 1.0001.000 for seed 11). With disjoint half-B samples, it ranges from 0.9690.969 to 1.0001.000; the shuffled reward’s alignment remains near zero; and the fraction of the update outside VV ranges from 0.620.62 to 0.980.98. In seed 11, the α=5\alpha=5 configuration declines from peak 0.270.27 to 0.1550.155, while the low-weight configuration gains +0.07+0.07. The two high-weight probe runs’ drops, 0.1000.100 and 0.1150.115, are below the descriptive 0.150.15 event threshold. These observations show that agreement with the reference persists even as greedy accuracy falls.

Credit on segments where continuations disagree. At initialization, 1212 prompts with four completions each are cut at eight interior points plus the endpoint, yielding 432432 segments and 2,5922{,}592 continuations at K=6K=6. Credit magnitude is |p^s−p^s−1||\widehat{p}_{s}-\widehat{p}_{s-1}|, with p^0=0.5\widehat{p}_{0}=0.5. A continuation-success variance above 0.10.1 means at least one success and one failure: the smallest nonzero variance at K=6K=6 is (1/6)​(5/6)=0.139(1/6)(5/6)=0.139. Such segments account for 19.7%19.7\% of segments and carry 38.4%38.4\% of credit; the remaining 61.6%61.6\% lies on unanimous segments. For disagreement segments, the ratio of credit share to segment share is 1.95×1.95\times, with correlation 0.300.30 and mean magnitude 0.220.22 versus 0.0850.085.

Shuffled-credit comparison. At α=5\alpha=5, the coherent and shuffled configurations use different rules for combining credit with the outcome; their paired difference-in-differences is −0.128-0.128 [−0.155,−0.098][-0.155,-0.098], dz=−3.46d_{z}=-3.46, over five common seeds. At α=4\alpha=4, both use the max-normalized rule, and the difference is −0.074-0.074 [−0.111,−0.040][-0.111,-0.040], dz=−1.62d_{z}=-1.62, n=5n=5, with gains −0.052-0.052 and +0.022+0.022 on that common-seed subset. Matching the rule removes one confound; the norms of the projected gradients, the clipping, the policy KL, and the Adam steps can still differ between the two configurations.

Length, entropy, and drift. On a fixed 100100-prompt subsample, response length stays within 1%1\% of the low-weight configuration through 2828 iterations while high-weight accuracy moves from 0.250.25 to 0.120.12; the fraction of degenerate completions does not rise. High-weight entropy rises from 0.210.21 to 0.580.58, versus 0.180.18–0.200.20 for low weight, and KL from the initial policy is about 3030 times larger. These changes occur together and are consistent with several optimization explanations, such as rising entropy or over-optimization of the proxy reward.

H.6 Other families, provers, reward sources, and datasets

To see whether the equal-iteration pattern depends on the model family, on where the progress estimates come from, or on the dataset, we repeat the comparison with each of them changed.

SmolLM3-3B. The same trainer uses HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM3-3B, with extended thinking disabled in the chat template. Outcome, α=0.5\alpha=0.5, and α=5\alpha=5 configurations were expanded to seeds 00–99 under a fixed paired-tt TOST analysis plan at ±0.03\pm 0.03 and one-sided harm test at 0.0050.005. The low-weight 90%90\% interval [−0.034,+0.005][-0.034,+0.005] excludes a gain of 0.030.03 (reported p=0.001p=0.001) and extends 0.0040.004 beyond the lower equivalence boundary. The high-weight paired effect is −0.092-0.092, dz=−0.77d_{z}=-0.77, one-sided p=0.02p=0.02, short of the specified 0.0050.005 criterion. Nine of ten differences are negative; two seeds drop 0.340.34 and 0.170.17 from peak, one ends at gain −0.267-0.267, and a third drop is 0.140.14. At α=2\alpha=2, one of three runs has a negative final gain. These results reproduce the qualitative pattern of the primary study at lower statistical resolution.

Complementary prover. A frozen Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct supplies continuations from the actor’s prefixes, following the complementary-prover motivation of Setlur et al. (2025); the actor receives the resulting dense credit. At α=1\alpha=1, three paired differences are +0.007,−0.040,+0.040+0.007,-0.040,+0.040, giving +0.002+0.002 [−0.040,+0.040][-0.040,+0.040]. A three-seed α=0.5\alpha=0.5 pilot gives +0.051+0.051 [+0.007,+0.100][+0.007,+0.100]. This was one of six exploratory comparisons. It motivated an n=8n=8 confirmation, which required a paired interval excluding zero and a result that passed Holm correction. The expanded estimate is +0.023+0.023 [−0.007,+0.052][-0.007,+0.052], dz=0.49d_{z}=0.49, from differences +0.100+0.100, +0.007+0.007, +0.047+0.047, −0.060-0.060, +0.020+0.020, +0.040+0.040, +0.027+0.027, +0.000+0.000. It falls short of the first criterion, and its interval still allows meaningful gains.

Step-labeled PRM. The frozen Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B (Zhang et al., 2025) scores actor-generated completions at the Monte-Carlo configuration’s interior cuts, using the step separator, canonical system prompt, and boxed-answer format. Differences in the PRM’s positive-class probabilities form a credit, with initial prior 0.50.5, combined with the outcome by the same rule. These differ from the model’s native double-newline step boundaries, which may weaken the reward. We rebuilt the scoring head from the released weights on a standard backbone; a convention check gives approximately 1.01.0 for correct chains and 0.00.0 for a corrupted step.

All 1616 planned PRM runs completed. At α=0.5\alpha=0.5, the paired effect is −0.009-0.009 [−0.049,+0.024][-0.049,+0.024], n=8n=8, superiority one-sided p=0.66p=0.66; TOST fails (plower=0.16p_{\mathrm{lower}}=0.16). At α=2\alpha=2, it is −0.090-0.090 [−0.125,−0.040][-0.125,-0.040], n=3n=3. At α=5\alpha=5, it is −0.133-0.133 [−0.188,−0.077][-0.188,-0.077], n=5n=5, one-sided p=0.007p=0.007, above the specified 0.0050.005 harm criterion. The latter two comparisons remain descriptive. These results apply to this conversion and scoring pipeline.

H.7 Degenerate-group channel ablation

Groups whose completions all fail give outcome-only GRPO no signal. Dense rewards are often motivated as a way to learn from such groups, whereas prompt selection (Section 4) avoids them, so we ask whether dense rewards help where they dominate. On a curated MATH slice, the fraction of groups with identical outcomes is 0.8940.894 (per-iteration range 0.500.50–1.001.00). Qwen2.5-1.5B is full-fine-tuned for 3232 iterations with group size eight, co-equal standardization, α=1\alpha=1, and seeds 00–22. The dense credit is zero-sum within each completion, which removes its completion-mean term but generally leaves a component in VV; at language-model scale, the measured component in VV carries about 0.260.26 of the squared norm. Outcome gains are +0.017,+0.009,+0.052+0.017,+0.009,+0.052 (mean +0.026+0.026), versus −0.070,+0.009,+0.009-0.070,+0.009,+0.009 (mean −0.017-0.017) for the dense-reward configuration. The paired effect is −0.043-0.043 [−0.087,0.000][-0.087,0.000] over three seeds (descriptive).

All completions in the degenerate groups are wrong to the reported precision, and training accuracy is about 0.020.02. Co-equal standardization amplifies a low-signal progress reward, and a frozen math-specialized prover succeeds on 13%13\% of 150150 tested prompts with k=4k=4, so progress is hard to estimate in this setting: where the outcome gradient is zero, a dense signal can exist without helping. Attributing the gains of other degenerate-group methods (Palandye et al., 2026; Agrawal et al., 2026) to a particular channel would need a control that trains only the completion-mean term.

NuminaMath. A 1,5001{,}500/200200 train/validation slice of NuminaMath-CoT uses the cn_k12 and synthetic-AMC sources, filtered to numeric answers supported by the verifier. It uses the same trainer for 3232 iterations and seeds 00–22; the outcome baseline gains +0.098+0.098 (Table 26). These rows use small samples and are descriptive.

I.1 What can a dense reward add to one update?

Outcome coefficients and completion means produce updates in VV (Propositions 2 and 3). The next result gives the exact condition under which a token-level credit stays in this space, accounting for the score map’s kernel: different token credits can produce the same gradient.

Theorem 1 (Sample-conditional equivalence).

For every credit ww,

grad(w)∈V⟺vec⁡(w)∈colspace⁡(B⊤)+ker⁡(S⊤).\begin{gathered}\operatorname{grad}(w)\in V\quad\Longleftrightarrow\\ \operatorname{vec}(w)\in\operatorname{colspace}(B^{\top})+\ker(S^{\top}).\end{gathered}

Moreover, dim(P⟂​S⊤​ker⁡B)=rank⁡(S)−dimV\dim\bigl(P_{\!\perp}S^{\top}\ker B\bigr)=\operatorname{rank}(S)-\dim V. If rank⁡(S)=G​H\operatorname{rank}(S)=GH, equivalence holds exactly for completion-constant credits, and the residual dimension is G⁡(H−1)G(H-1).

Centering credit within each completion does not generally make its gradient orthogonal to VV (Theorem 3). Once a credit adds a direction outside VV, we can ask whether that direction helps a local target.

Proposition 1 (First-order projection identity).

For arbitrary h=∇J​(θ)h=\nabla J(\theta) and dense direction d=grad⁡(w)d=\operatorname{grad}(w), the first-order advantage of dd over its matched projection PV​dP_{V}d is

⟨h,d−PV​d⟩=⟨P⟂​h,P⟂​d⟩.\langle h,d-P_{V}d\rangle=\langle P_{\!\perp}h,P_{\!\perp}d\rangle.

Only the components of dd and hh outside VV decide whether dd improves on its projection to first order. This is the alignment test of Section 2.4, which Section 3.1 measures against a sampled reference. It compares a direction with its own projection at one policy, whereas an outcome-only training run follows its own sequence of policies and sampled batches.

Proof of Proposition 1.

The complementary orthogonal projectors are self-adjoint and satisfy PV​P⟂=0P_{V}P_{\!\perp}=0. Thus ⟨h,d⟩=⟨PV​h,PV​d⟩+⟨P⟂​h,P⟂​d⟩\langle h,d\rangle=\langle P_{V}h,P_{V}d\rangle+\langle P_{\!\perp}h,P_{\!\perp}d\rangle. Subtracting the rate of PV​dP_{V}d proves the identity. We do not need to represent hh through the finite sampled matrix. If we use an estimator h^\widehat{h}, the rate error satisfies

|⟨P⟂​(h^−h),P⟂​d⟩|≤‖h^−h‖​‖P⟂​d‖.\big|\langle P_{\!\perp}(\widehat{h}-h),P_{\!\perp}d\rangle\big|\leq\|\widehat{h}-h\|\,\|P_{\!\perp}d\|.

An empirical alignment measurement alone does not bound this estimation error. ∎

K.1.1 Telescoping is not confinement

Take one two-token completion with linearly independent scores s1,s2s_{1},s_{2}. The credit w=(1,−1)w=(1,-1) has zero total, yet s1−s2∉span⁡{s1+s2}=Vs_{1}-s_{2}\notin\operatorname{span}\{s_{1}+s_{2}\}=V. It can represent the potential increments along a path with values 0,1,00,1,0. Broadcasting the total instead produces the zero credit in VV. Potential-based shaping results concern particular reward, return and baseline constructions (Ng et al., 1999); a telescoping total alone does not constrain the sampled score sum weighted by token coefficients. Likewise, when all group rewards agree, A=0A=0 and the outcome update is zero, but this does not guarantee that a nonzero dense update improves JJ.

Appendix L The Expected GRPO Update

The results of Appendix I describe one sampled batch. This section gives the expected outcome-only GRPO update over fresh samples, which the matched-compute methods use to explain how adding a dense reward can change the relative weight of prompts (Appendix C).

L.1 The population gradient is not confined to a sampled span

Proposition 4 (Expected binary group-relative score).

Fix a prompt and a differentiable distribution over completions. Assume its support is independent of the parameters and that differentiation can pass under the expectation. Let R⁡(τ)∈{0,1}R(\tau)\in\{0,1\} be a fixed verifier, p⁡(θ)=𝔼​R∈(0,1)p(\theta)=\mathbb{E}R\in(0,1), G≥2G\geq 2, and sample completions iid. Define qg=∇log⁡πθ​(τg)q_{g}=\nabla\log\pi_{\theta}(\tau_{g}), KR=∑gRgK_{R}=\sum_{g}R_{g}, and let sks_{k} be the group reward standard deviation when KR=kK_{R}=k. With advantages equation 1,

𝔼[1G∑gAgqg]=λG(p)∇p,λG​(p)=𝔼⁡[KR​(G−KR)/(G2​(sKR+ϵ))]p⁡(1−p)>0.\begin{gathered}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{g}A_{g}q_{g}\right]=\lambda_{G}(p)\nabla p,\\ \lambda_{G}(p)=\frac{\mathbb{E}[K_{R}(G-K_{R})/(G^{2}(s_{K_{R}}+\epsilon))]}{p(1-p)}>0.\end{gathered} (6)

Groups with KR∈{0,G}K_{R}\in\{0,G\} contribute zero.

Proof.

The score identity gives 𝔼​q=0\mathbb{E}q=0 and 𝔼⁡[R​q]=∇p\mathbb{E}[Rq]=\nabla p, hence 𝔼[q∣R=1]=∇p/p\mathbb{E}[q\mid R=1]=\nabla p/p and 𝔼[q∣R=0]=−∇p/(1−p)\mathbb{E}[q\mid R=0]=-\nabla p/(1-p). Condition on KR=kK_{R}=k. By exchangeability, the expected sums of successful and failed completion scores are k∇p/pk\nabla p/p and −(G−k)∇p/(1−p)-(G-k)\nabla p/(1-p). Their advantage coefficients are (G−k)/(G⁡(sk+ϵ))(G-k)/(G(s_{k}+\epsilon)) and −k/(G(sk+ϵ))-k/(G(s_{k}+\epsilon)). Substituting these values and applying the outer 1/G1/G gives

𝔼[1G∑gAgqg|KR=k]=k⁡(G−k)G2​(sk+ϵ)​p​(1−p)∇p.\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{g}A_{g}q_{g}\,\middle|\,K_{R}=k\right]=\frac{k(G-k)}{G^{2}(s_{k}+\epsilon)p(1-p)}\nabla p.

Averaging proves the formula. Since p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1) and G≥2G\geq 2, a mixed group has positive probability. The multiplier is therefore positive. At p=0p=0 or p=1p=1, all sampled advantages are zero and the displayed ratio is undefined. ∎

This score-function identity does not identify a new obstacle to population learning. Population GRPO analyses also study the normalization and success dynamics (Mroueh, 2026). Across prompts, λG​(p)\lambda_{G}(p) can vary and reweight their gradients. Bias from clipping, off-policy sampling or other transformations needs a separate analysis. An update can belong to its sampled VV without its expectation belonging to any one realized VV.
